speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to amend the Bank of Canada Act so as to increase the capital stock of the bank, to provide that certain shares thereof shall be purchased by the Minister of Finance out of the consolidated revenue fund in order to assure ownership of a majority of the shares by the government, to increase the number of directors, and to provide for election and appointment of directors in such manner as to assure voting control of the board by directors appointed by the government.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this resolution precedes the introduction of a bill which will provide for certain important amendments to the Bank of Canada Act, in order to implement the announcement made in the speech from the throne that parliament would be asked to make such changes in the ownership and control of the Bank of Canada as may be necessary to give to the government a predominant interest in the ownership as well as effective control of the bank.
The bill which this resolution seeks authority to introduce provides among other things for two important and significant changes in the constitution of the Bank of Canada. These changes are: First, the issue of an additional
85,100,000	of capital stock of the bank, to be purchased by the Minister of Finance and held by him on behalf of the Dominion of Canada. This will ensure a predominance of public ownership in the shares of our central bank. Second, the appointment by the government of additional directors of the bank with sufficient voting power to give the government a majority control of the board of directors both immediately and permanently.
There are other changes of lesser importance in the bill to be introduced. Most of these are consequent upon the changes in the capital stock and in the directorate to which I have just referred, but others are being made to clear up ambiguities in the wording of the present act or to provide for changes which experience has shown to be desirable. I might call special attention to one other amendment, which provides that Bank of Canada notes in future will be bilingual instead of some being printed in the English language and some in the French language, as at present.
I should like now to discuss the factors which have led the government to propose amendments to the constitution of the bank providing for a predominant interest by the public in the ownership and also voting control of the bank. In the first place, the fundamental consideration is that the primary function of a central bank is to regulate the volume of currency and credit in use, and this

Bank of Canada

institutions free from effective government control. The Bank of France is in fact subject to-day to a degree of such control.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext: So is the Bank of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
Yes. Finally, the matter of public ownership is in my opinion much less important than that of governmental control. If we study the constitution of central banks from this aspect we shall find ample precedent for the attempt which we are making to give the government adequate control over the Bank of Canada.
It is not possible or necessary to consider all the precedents. I wish however to draw attention to the constitution of a number of typical important central banks, and particularly to those in some of the other British dominions.
The Bank of England is of course not only privately owned, but also completely free from formal governmental control. The board, consisting of the governor, deputy governor and twenty-four directors, is elected annually by the shareholders. The English statute was passed at a time when individualism was the guiding doctrine in political and economic theory, and to have given the government control over the bank would have been in complete conflict with all the teachings of that day. Nevertheless, as Kisch and Elkin point out:
There can be little doubt that in practice there is at all times close and continuous cooperation between the bank and the government, and in exceptional periods of stress there is even more than this.
The Reichsbank, the central bank of Germany, is under its present constitution the only other important instance of a leading central bank which, at least on paper is, independent of its central government. The original Reichsbank, which dates back to the founding of the German empire, w'as subject to a high degree of governmental control. The supervisory powers of the state were exercised by a board appointed by the emperor and the federal council-Bundersrat or Senate-whose chairman ex-officio, was the imperial chancellor. The general management of the bank was entrusted to the chancellor, to whom the board of directors was subordinate. The members of the board were appointed by the emperor on the recommendation of the federal council.
Following upon the post-war inflation the Reichsbank was reorganized in 1924, and this reorganization was, to quote Kisch and Elkin:
Part and parcel of a scheme for the payment .of reparations and of the financial rehabilitation
of Germany devised by foreign experts at a time when the financial policy of the German government was politically suspect and had proved to be economically unsound.
The act as a result shows a distrust of government influence which would probably not have been so manifest had the reorganization come from entirely within Germany, instead of partly from outside. In the case of the Bank of France the general council consists of the governor, two deputy governors, fifteen regents and three auditors. The regents and auditors are elected by the general assembly consisting of the two hundred largest shareholders, chosen from certain specified economic classes. The governor and deputy governors are appointed and removable by the President of France on the recommendation of the Minister of Finance. No decision of the general council may be executed unless it bears the signature of the governor. In the final analysis it is the government-appointed governor who directs all the bank's business and exercises the final power.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
The Bank of Russia, as one would suspect, is a complete state bank managed by a board of directors appointed by the government and supervised by the People's Commissary of Finances. So also is the Bank of Finland, which carries on its business under the guarantee and supervision of the diet. The state owned central bank of Sweden is managed by a board of directors appointed by the king or the riksdag, the one director appointed by the king acting as the president of the bank, and these directors are responsible to the riksdag, its parliamentary committee on banking, and its auditors alone. In the case of Norway, the central bank is privately owned but the private shareholders have no control of the administration and no provision is made for general meetings. Three members of the board of directors and the members of the supervisory council are nominated by parliament, while the governor and vice governor are nominated by the king. In Spain the appointment of the members of the council has always required state approval,

Bank oj Canada
and since 1931 the council has included three government appointees, to represent the general interest of the national economy. The governor, who is executive head of the bank, is nominated by the government and is given power to suspend any decision of the council that he considers contrary to the laws and report it to the finance minister. The Swiss National Bank has a council of forty members, of which twenty-five including the president and vice president, are government appointees, nominated by the federal council.
But government control is not limited to the appointment of governors or of a proportion of the directors. Kisch and Elkin, the authorities on the structure and functioning of central banks, cite a number of instances where more direct supervision may be exercised by the state in certain circumstances. Thus in Italy the finance minister, in addition to supervising the note issue, may annul any decision of the general meeting of the administrative council which he considers contrary to the laws and statutes, acting on his own initiative or on the report of a government official designated by him to attend the meetings of these bodies. In the charters of a number of European central banks, including those of Austria, Poland. Greece, Hungary, Holland and Denmark, there is provision for the appointment of a government or royal commissioner, with supervisory powers. Generally the duties of these commissioners are limited to seeing that the bank's business is carried on in accordance with the law and statutes of the bank. On any disputed point, the commissioner has a suspensory veto until the matter is settled by agreement between the bank and the government. In Denmark, the finance ministry must be notified when the bank's managers wish to change the rate of discount; the minister is entitled to participate personally or by deputy in the discussion but without the right to vote. In Poland, the president of the bank, who is appointed by the president of the republic, has a right of suspensory veto in respect of decisions of the bank council which are, in his opinion, contrary to the laws of the country, the articles of association of the bank or the interests of the state. When he exercises this right of veto, the question is referred to the finance minister, and the contemplated action is not carried out if the president's veto is endorsed by the minister within three days.
In Czechoslovakia, a government commissioner, chosen from officials of the finance ministry, has the right of suspensory veto over any resolution of the bank's managerial bodies if they appear in conflict with the
laws, statutes or state interests. Failing agreement between the bank and the government, the matter must be referred to a committee of arbitration. In Roumania, the government commissioner has the right of intervention in regard to any decision by the bank's executive which he considers inimical to state interests. In Japan, government control of the central bank goes to great lengths. Comptrollers acting under direction of the finance minister supervise all matters connected with the Bank of Japan. Wide powers of intervention are reserved to the government, and the decisions of the administrative board are subject, in various important instances, to government approval before they become effective. The bank's by-laws provide that "the government shall control all the operations of the bank and shall prevent not only any operation which conflicts with the act and by-laws, but also any measure that the government may deem disadvantageous to the state."	*
We may now turn to the central banks of the British dominions. Perhaps these have more lessons to teach Canada because of their comparatively recent establishment, their freedom from accidental developments due to war or other historical circumstances, and also of course the broad similarity of prevailing political and economic philosophies and conditions with those of our own country.
The oldest of these institutions is the Commonwealth Bank of Australia. Founded in 1912, this bank is wholly government owned and operates under government guarantee. The board consists of the governor and seven other directors, including the secretary to the treasury. The governor, deputy governor and directors are all appointed by the government.
The Reserve Bank of South Africa, organized in 1920, is owned in part by the commercial banks and in part by private shareholders. Its board consists of the governor and deputy governor, both appointed by the government, and of nine other directors of whom three are appointed by the government and six are elected by the shareholders.
The Reserve Bank of New Zealand, which commenced operations only a few months before the Bank of Canada, is a privately owned bank but with government representation on its board. The board consists of the governor, the deputy governor, the secretary to the treasury (without the power to vote), and seven other directors. As in the case of the Bank of Canada, the first governor and deputy governor are appointed by the government, while later governors and deputy
Bank oj Canada

governors are appointed by the government on the recommendation of the board of directors. Of the seven other directors three are government appointees, while the remaining four are elected by the shareholders, except the initial four who also were appointed by the government. It will thus be seen that the first board of this bank is entirely composed of government appointees. Under the present legislation, however, the board would ultimately consist of two governors approved by the government, the secretary to the treasury, three government appointed directors and four directors elected by shareholders. As hon. members of the committee are aware, the present government of New Zealand has announced its intention of introducing a greater measure of government control of the bank.
The constitution of the new Reserve Bank of India provides for a central board consisting of the governor, four government nominees [DOT]representative of territorial, economic or agricultural interests, and eight directors elected from the elected members of the local boards of the five reserve banking areas in certain proportions. Deputy governors and one government official will also be on the central board but without voting rights. The central board can be superseded by another agency for direction of the bank's affairs under government orders, in the event, of the bank failing to carry out any of the obligations imposed on it. The governor and deputy governors are appointed by the government, on advice of the central board.
It is of interest to note that government control extends farther in each of these empire central banks than at present in Canada, and in some cases, substantially farther.
So much for the argument based on history and the experience of other countries. The brief review which I have given should be sufficient to show that ample sound precedent exists for the amendments to the present Bank of Canada Act, now under consideration.
A second type of argument used by my predecessor in advocating the present constitution of the Bank of Canada was that based on the opinions of monetary experts or the resolutions passed by international conferences. I do not propose to call experts to rebut experts, although that would not be difficult to do. Someone has said that "where five economists are gathered together there will be found six opinions, and two of them wiil belong to Mr. Keynes." It is sufficient to say that the examples of government ownership and control of central banks which I have cited above must rest on adequate expert opinion and on the bedrock of experi-

ence of other countries and nations. However, considerable stress was laid on a resolution passed at the international financial conference held at Brussels in 1920, and reiterated in a later international conference, and it may be well to say a word with regard to that. The resolution is as follows:
Banks, and especially banks of issue, should be freed from political pressure and should be conducted solely on the lines of prudent finance.
It is desirable to consider the setting in which this resolution was drawn. It was passed just after the war at a time of monetary chaos and currency depreciation when central banks of many countries, whether government owned or government controlled or not, were stiff busy turning out paper money and inflating bank credit under the direction of their respective governments. The admonition which it gave against influences and against imprudent financing is a natural one and fully warranted under the circumstances then prevailing. But surely we do not need to be warned to-day of the utter folly of printing press methods of finance. I have already shown, I think, that the historical record shows no coincidence between the prudently versus imprudently managed central banks on the one hand and the privately owned and controlled versus government owned and. controlled central banks on the other.
This brings me to the third argument of my predecessor, Hon. Mr. Rhodes, namely, the charge that a central bank under government control would be subject to political influence, to the puff and the pressure of this group or that, to political interference in its day to day operations, and to partisan influence in appointments. I might make two comments in regard to that argument.
In the first place there is a type of influence, using the word in its broadest and best sense, to which the Bank of Canada should be subject. I have already shown that the bank is required to perform one of the most important functions of government. The wise and efficient carrying out of that function is of vital concern to every citizen. Under some other form of government we might be content with a privately owned and controlled institution acting as a benevolent despot, answerable to no authority but itself, unresponsive to public opinion, giving the public not what they want but what the experts think is right for them. But that attitude is not possible in a democratic country. The bank may and should resist temporary gusts of public fancy, but in the long run it must show responsiveness to public opinion. In the long run the bank in the performance of a vital sovereign

function must be responsible to the sovereign will expressed through governments. There cannot be two sovereigns in a single state. In that connection nothing I think could be clearer than the statement of the present Prime Minister, then leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), taken from Hansard of June 22, 1934, page 4227:
I want to make this fact clear: no one could have had the responsibility of being the head of an administration for any time without realizing all that it meant when one speaks of political pressure. I think I would be the first to sympathize with the Prime Minister in his desire so to frame an act that what is termed political pressure would not be permitted to interfere with the successful and independent working of a great financial institution. May I say we may give a wholly wrong meaning to the word ' political" in speaking of political pressure. A political influence or point of view is not necessarily something that is contrary to the national interest; a political point of view is one which arises from an endeavour to give expression to public feeling and public opinion, and I submit that in all democratic countries public opinion is the one great factor for which all governments must have consideration. There are times when it is necessary and vital that every institution in the land should be subject to the public opinion of the nation, and this is always the case when it is expressed in a constitutional way in parliament. I do not believe powers should be given any institution that would enable it to put itself in a position of opposition to a government that has been entrusted with great responsibilities of enforcing particular policies.
In the same speech on the same day, Hansard, page 4228, the right hon. gentleman (Mr. Mackenzie King) said:
What I should like to ask is:	Are the
institutions created by governments themselves to be made by their very constitutions so powerful that in the matter of national policies they can regard themselves as wholly beyond the direction of a government, where those policies are the result of the will of the people as expressed by their representatives in parliament? In no way could it be possible to have more clearly defined the difference between the right hon. gentleman opposite and myself. The Prime Minister will notice that at the moment, I am not suggesting the government should own the bank. I am not at the moment discussing the question of ownership, at all. As I said last night, I think the question of ownership is debatable. I am however discussing the question of control of policy, and I do say that with respect to policies, whether they relate to trade, to shipping, to marketing, to finance, to defence, or to any other phase of a country's economy, those policies, if they are the expression of view of a government representative of the people, should be capable of being carried out without interference from any institution whatever, but rather with the sympathetic cooperation of all institutions. That is the only way in which in a country we can have either democratic or responsible government.
In the second place, the criticism in so far as it relates to partisan interference in appointments and political interference in day
Bank oj Canada
to day operations, and in so far as it is meant to apply to the Bank of Canada, is wholly beside the point. No one proposes that the government should concern itself with minor appointments or with the routine of daily operations. The first governor and deputy governor are, in the present act and in the act as it will be amended, appointed by the governor in council; later appointments to these two positions will be made by the board of directors subject to the approval of the governor in council. I am sure no member of the committee need have any fear that such appointments will be subject to political pressure or to partisan influences. We may safely assume, in my opinion, that these two officials, who are the chief executive officers of the bank and responsible for its detailed, day to day administration, will be appointed on grounds of merit only, particularly with the safeguard provided by the act that they in future are to be nominated by the board of directors and approved by the governor in council.
There remain the government-appointed directors. The bill which it is proposed to introduce will provide for four such directors. For the next four years these government directors will have two votes each. If the government is to secure an immediate majority control of the board, this dual voting provision is necessary, because it is not intended to disturb the present elected directors, numbering seven, until their terms ^ of office expire. As their terms of office expire, they will drop out and not be replaced, except that the private shareholders shall always have the right to elect three directors. After the annual general meeting in 1940 the board will consist of these three elected directors, four government-appointed directors (each with a single vote), the governor and deputy governor (both government-appointed or approved), and the Deputy Minister of Finance (without the power to vote).
This type of board, it is submitted, will achieve the objectives which the government desires without being open to the objections which have been directed against the constitution of the present board. It will, for instance, provide for a predominant interest by the government in the general administration of an institution which is charged with responsibility for performing a vital national function. It will not mean that the government will be concerned with the daily routine management of the bank, but rather that the government will be assured that the direction of the bank is in the hands of men in whose judgment it has confidence. Since the appointments of directors are for limited terms only, a long
Bank of Canada

continuance of a policy that might conflict with the government's view becomes impossible.
Moreover, it will prevent the sort of fiasco which took place at the time of the first election of directors. It will be remembered that the act placed on the shareholders a task which in my opinion was exceedingly difficult, if not impossible, for them to carry out. Seven directors were to be elected by an unorganized group of over 12,000 shareholders scattered throughout the whole of Canada. Moreover, these directors were to be "selected from diversified occupations," and, while the act did not so state, it was essential in the national interest that they should also be reasonably representative of the various geographic sections of the country as well as of the two chief racial groups. What in fact happened, as you well know, was that the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, an organized business group, intervened in the election and submitted a slate of nominees bearing its recommendation. The result was that every nominee on this slate was elected. Please understand that I am not criticizing the personnel of the present board of directors. On the contrary, I believe that the country is fortunate in securing the services of those now acting in this capacity. What I am pointing out, and criticizing most severely, is legislation which in practice permits a private business association in effect to name the directors of our central bank. That is, in my opinion, an intolerable situation.

Under the proposed amendments the private shareholders will not have to elect more than one director in any one year and, having in mind the occupations and geographic sections represented by these directors, the government will be able to select its four appointed directors in such a manner as to provide a board which is reasonably representative of all the important national interests which the Bank of Canada has to serve.
It seems to me also that the presence on the board of two types of directors-those appointed by the government and those elected by the shareholders-will have distinct advantages. In developing this argument, I can do no better than quote from a statement made by the present Prime Minister, then leader of the opposition, on June 22, 1934, in this house, 
on the second reading of the Bank of Canada bill. This statement appears on page 4228 of Hansard of that year, and reads:
I say that power of influence of governments and defiance of governments by the money power is being created by this act in the form in which it is at present, and the only way in which that possibility can be avoided is for the government to see to it that, on the board of directors who are to direct this institution, there are representatives of the government, who will not own any of the shares, but who will be the appointees of the government placed there solely to watch and safeguard the public interest. I think my right hon. friend must agree that in these matters of large finance, check and counter check is -wholly advisable. It is advisable in financial transactions of a limited size, and it is more necessary as well as advisable in those of considerable size. But here are financial transactions of the greatest magnitude conceivable, and check and counter check are imperative. I do think the directorate of the bank ought to be so formed that, whether the pressure is upon the bank from the government on the one side, or upon the government from the financial interests and through the bank on the other, there should be on the board of directors some one or more persons who will be quick to sense the situation, give the danger signal, and arouse the country to the pressure which is being brought to bear. There is the danger of a government bringing too much in the way of pressure to bear on a central bank. On the other hand, there is equal danger of the financial interests that are allied with the banks bringing influence to bear upon a government. There will be both these dangers always, and the only way in which that possibility can be lessened is by making sure that both powers, the money power and the power of government, are represented on a common board so that one or the other will be in a position to direct the attention of the people at large to the dangers which they may see developing in the affairs of an institution which is or ought to be a great national trust.
As I have stated already, the amendments proposed are not such as to involve interference by the government in the daily routine administration of the bank, or the possibility of partisan influence in minor appointments. According to the act, the government, "shall be the chief executive officer and shall on behalf of the board have the direction and control of the business of the bank, with authority to act in connection with the conduct of the business in all matters which are not by this act or by the by-laws of the bank specifically reserved to be done by the board or by the executive committee, or by a meeting of shareholders."

Another limitation was that the dividends payable to shareholders should be limited to 4J per cent. It may be well in passing to point out that in the first ten months of the operation of the new central bank, after providing for the necessary rest and reserves and all other matters of the kind, there was paid into the consolidated revenue fund of the dominion as profit from the operation of the bank the sum of $346,184.33.

I should like to go a step further. Let me point out how the right hon. gentleman indicated he was going to discharge "the most conspicuous and sacred responsibility of government." I turn to a report of a speech of the right hon. gentleman contained in the Vancouver Sun of September 30, 1935. I imagine most hon. members of this committee are familiar with the fact that the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation was pretty well in its stride in Vancouver, and is reported so to be in British Columbia. Out there the right hon. gentleman had this to say:
"We believe that credit should be a social service to serve the needs of the people."
"Credit is not the concern of the bankers only but is of concern to you and me."
Credit is to-day controlled by the great international money power. The first step, then, is to establish a national central bank -not another private bank as has been done -but a government bank able to control credit according to the will of the government in matters of great national concern.
The Liberal party believes it is a public matter of direct concern to the average citizen to have a national bank to control currency and credit so that they may serve the public needs.
The first objective is to get back the control that was taken from us. The next is to see that the bank is made national in the truest sense of the word."
Now in fulfilment of that pledge and obligation the government headed by the right hon. gentleman brings forward this anaemic measure providing for a half nationally and half privately-owned central bank w'hieh is to discharge "the most conspicuous and sacred responsibilities of government."
Then the right hon. gentleman went to Alberta where the social credit group appears
to have been in its stride. According to a report in the Calgary Daily Herald of October 1, 1935, the right hon. gentleman said:
"A central bank is necessary to determine the supply of currency in relation to domestic, social and industrial requirements of the Canadian people, and also to deal with problems of international commerce and exchange."
So far the leader of the social credit group might have been making the speech. The right hon. gentleman continued:
"That was a clear statement"-
He was referring to a statement he had made previously.
-"that what we wanted at Ottawa was a central bank, or wanted in Canada, was a central national bank which would enable private banks to be controlled by the central institution in a manner which would make credit be considered more from the point of public need, domestic requirements, social requirements, and the like, than from the point of view of the interests of capital investors and private bankers oniy."
Then he went on.
"Then the government policy, if it were one of extension of credit, would be in a position to put that policy into effect"-
That must be a misprint, because I doubt whether the right hon. gentleman would have repeated the word "policy." I continue:
-"through having a central bank which would give more in the way of credit at the time when the need for more in the way of credit was uppermost. It would regulate credit in a manner which would serve the needs of the country, prevent excessive speculation on the one hand, and on the other hand help serve to increase the currency and the facilities for credit when need for increased currency and increased credit facilities were required."
And then this last touch, which I think is sublime.
"We have in the federal field the great issue of monetary reform. I have merely indicated what I have thought was the first step, and if that first is not won then all our efforts at further financial reform so far as the federal field is concerned will be materially impaired."
"Equally"-
Says the right hon. gentleman to the electors of Alberta.
-"if they are materially impaired it will have a very serious effect as far as I see it upon the efforts of any province to improve financial conditions there, so I hope when Monday fortnight comes you will think not only what is important to you locally and in a provincial way, but that you will think even more deeply of what is going to be of vital concern to our country with respect to our policy during the next five years."
I leave it to the judgment of hon. members of the committee and the people of the country
Bank of Canada

whether the present proposal for a nationally owned central bank, which is neither meat nor fish, flesh nor fowl, is the first step in a great monetary reform in Canada.
I am not sure whether the right hon. gentleman went back to Vancouver, but in any event he made another speech which was fully reported in the Vancouver Province of September 21, 1935. In that speech he said:
"Canada is faced with a great battle between the money power and the power of the people *-a battle which will be waged in the next parliament. He pleaded for a sweeping liberal majority in order to carry out his policy of public control of currency and credit, nationalization of the Bank of Canada and monetary reform."
I suppose monetary reform is bo follow this half measure of nationalization. The right hon. gentleman went on to say:
The battle whieh would be fought in parliament would decide whether "we are going to have the money power bend to the will of the people."
He finished his observation by saying:
"Until the control and issue of currency and credit is restored to the government and recognized as its most conspicuous and sacred responsibility, all talk of the sovereignty of parliament and democracy is idle and futile."
Well, the people gave the right hon. gentleman a sweeping Liberal majority, and we are here to-day in the arena ready for the great monetary battle. The right hon. gentleman says he is the gladiator who will champion the cause of the people, that he recognizes the control of currency as the most conspicuous and sacred responsibility of government. But where is the money power with which he is going to do battle? It was the private interests which owned the central bank. Are those private interests, with which the right hon. gentleman was going to do battle, wiped out by this measure? Oh, no! I suggest he is a prudent man. Instead of having them do battle in the arena of parliament he compromises by saying, We will permit you to keep your stock in the central bank; we will continue to pay you four and a half per cent dividend, the maximum amount you can receive if the bank makes money; we will avoid pitched battle in parliament, and by your ownership of forty-nine per cent of the stock of the central bank you are still in possession of forty-nine per cent of the assets. Is it any wonder the electors of Canada were misled? And not only the electors; is it any wonder the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) believed he was supporting a party which had a policy embracing his ideas? How well I remember that gentleman coming as a new member to this parliament, with 
high hopes for the government he was supporting and with that great confidence and faith which led him to stand in his place and say:
"The government must have time to adopt policies which will enable them to provide the money before we can expect them to bring in such legislation."
Then, after proposing that the Bank of Canada should advance whatever money the country may need against dominion, municipal and provincial bonds, he said:
"I venture to stand in my place to-day and make these suggestions as a Liberal because our great leader has taken the attitude that people of all shades of opinion will be welcome within the ranks of the Liberal party."
Mr. Chairman, can you blame the hon. member for Rosthern for drawing any such conclusion in view of the utterances of his leader upon the stump in this country during the last campaign? But he still had faith, this hon. member for Rosthern, and several others like him in the Liberal fold in this house, because speaking later, at page 552 of Hansard for this session, he enunciated just what most of the electorate believed, that what the Liberal party was advocating was an absolute and complete nationally owned central bank, as stated by the Minister of National Defence in this house in 1934; because the hon. member for Rosthern stood up in his place this session and said, "I am one hundred per cent in favour of a one hundred per cent ownership and control of the Bank of Canada by the Canadian people through our government." No room for mistake in that; and then he finished up by saying: "That, in short, Mr. Speaker, is the view I think of at least fifty per cent of the Liberal voters in this country." I ask again, does this measure, half private, half public ownership, meet their views? Will the hon. gentleman and all the others like him who sit in the ranks of the Liberal party in this house get up on their feet in this discussion and tell us whether they believed that their leader was standing for a one hundred per cent publicly owned central bank when he came down here and enunciated his views and his theories? And will they tell us they consider that this measure is discharging "that most conspicuous and sacred responsibility" to which the right hon. gentleman so frequently referred when he was seeking the franchise of the people of this country?

I would congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) upon his very clear statement, and also the government upon having taken a position that is in advance of that which now exists, namely, the banking policy of the Conservative party, and which also represents somewhat of an advance upon any definite position hitherto taken by the Liberal party. I say the latter although I recognize clearly that a number of members of the Liberal party have gone much further than this legislation goes.
It seems to me there are several questions with regard to public finance that have been before the people of this country. One is, should there be a central bank? For a long time both the old parties were very skeptical with regard to the necessity of a central bank, and even went so far as to denounce anything of that nature. The second is, how should this central bank be owned and controlled? It was on that point that we had a good deal of difference of opinion when the present act was introduced.
There is a third consideration upon which the old parties seem agreed, and on which we in this comer differ from both, and that is we favour the nationalization of our financial institutions, including both the central bank and the chartered banks. Again and again we have introduced resolutions along that line only to be defeated by a joint vote of both the two old parties.
May I call attention to the position that we in this comer have taken throughout the years? As early as 1923 I emphasized the monopolistic character of the banking system of this country, and I pointed out that by virtue of the private ownership of this monopoly, financial control and credit are used in disregard of social considerations, prices can be and are manipulated by the control of quantity purchasing power, and finally I said that we must find a remedy in the public control of currency and credit. You will find my speech in Hansard of 1923, page 4018.
In 1925 I ventured to bring forward this motion:
That, in the opinion of this house, it is not in the interests of the country at large that the privilege of issuing currency and of controlling financial credit should be granted to private corporations.
When I listened to the finance minister to-day I began to feel that some of us in this comer had not altogether wasted our energies. In those days we had comparatively little support from those who now occupy the government benches or from those who now occupy the position of official
opposition. We feel that the Minister of Finance is right when he recognizes the influence of public opinion. Undoubtedly public opinion has been driving the Liberal party.
In that same year, speaking of the quantity of money, after quoting Professor Taussig, I said:
How is that regulated to-day? It is regulated by the banks. . . . They do so either directly through the giving or withholding of credit or in their control over government policy. ... I urge that the large measures of control of currency and credit by private corporations now existing must not continue. It is not safe to leave such power in private, and shall I say, without offence, irresponsible hands, that is, in the hands of those without responsibility to the people at large.
I continued:
Is it wise to leave this power in the hands of private individuals who can exercise their control in their own economic and political interests, disregarding the effect on the welfare of the general population? Why shouldn't the government democratically control this money situation rather than allow a group of a dozen men who are not responsible to our people to do so? We now have government supervision and inspection. We have had the advocacy of government guarantee of deposits. . . . From all over the country demands are coming in that the government should go much farther than it has in the past. Why not take the next step and effectively control our currency and credit?
The minister now says that that is necessary and he proposes this resolution as the forerunner of a bill which he thinks will make that possible. I might add that we in our group again and again moved resolutions for the establishment of a national system of banking. I myself introduced one in 1925 and down through the years we have tried to emphasize the need of a national banking system.
When the present act was up for discussion the Liberals were by no means certain of their position. They did unite to criticize the measure, but the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said it was rather debatable whether or not the bank should be publicly owned and controlled. Some of his followers had no such hesitation. It will be remembered that some of them came out very strongly for an absolutely publicly owned and publicly controlled bank. Hon. members will recall that famous amendment to the effect that the bank should be either publicly owned and privately controlled, privately owned and publicly controlled, or, publicly owned and publicly controlled. As it was considered that the mover of that resolution represented the Liberal party, I say that the government has been very vacillating and

very temporizing. I was much interested in noting the position once taken by the present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler). We find the following on page 453 of Hansard of 1935:
As the house knows very well, and as I think the country knows, though the people may just as well be reminded of the fact for fear of misrepresentation afterwards, we on this side of the house were last year almost entirely in favour of a publicly owned central bank, though we may not be inclined, at least now-I am speaking for myself

to go as far as the nationalization of the chartered banks of Canada.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce felt that Liberals were almost entirely in favour of a publicly owned central bank. I do not think there is the slightest doubt that the hon. member for York South is correct when he says that was the impression given by the majority of Liberal speakers during the last campaign. The Minister of Trade and Commerce is also reported on page 454 as follows:
I did not intend to take up so much of the time of the house and did so for only two reasons: first, the aspersion-and I think I may call it that, which was cast by the Prime Minister and again by the Minister of Finance upon the integrity and strength of character that ought to animate any government that has the interests of the people at heart, in suggesting that they could not properly and honestly administer the functions that naturally belong to a central bank. In the second place I want to put myself on record that I have not retreated and I do not think those on this side have retreated from the position we took last year that we are entirely in favour of a publicly owned and controlled central bank of Canada.
Surely that is a pretty clear statement. I said a few moments ago that I did not think the Liberal speakers gave the impression to the people that they were going to get any such legislation as this. On the contrary, the people generally understood that they were to have a thoroughgoing	publicly	owned and	publicly
controlled bank. In this connection I should like to quote from the Regina-Leader Post of May 18, which reports a meeting of the Young Liberal executive of Saskatoon, as follows:
Dealing	specifically with the central bank
question,	the	Young Liberal	executivestressed that one of the chief planks in the platform on which the Liberal party was elected to power at Ottawa was the establishment of	"a	properly	constituted	national

Therefore, this executive of the Saskatoon Young Men's Liberal Club, expresses its

The minister stated to-day that the naming of tfie directors of the central bank by private individuals was intolerable, but I should like to ask him whether it is any better that the dividends of our central bank should go to private individuals. A situation such as confronts Canada recently confronted the government of New Zealand. It seems that everything that has been, done in this house up to date has rested entirely upon this monetary question. Such momentous questions as pensions for the blind, relief of the unemployment situation, and public works inevitably revert to the problem of money; yet we allow this debate to be the last or one of the last matters brought up in the house. I think it is time that this subject should be taken up fully. I commend the other speakers, especially the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation (Mr. Woodsworth) for their constructive ideas, because the true purpose of parliamentary debate is to provide constructive criticism.
I desire to make plain in the following language the position taken by the group with which I am associated, on the question of the nationalization of the central bank. We have no objection to the public ownership of this bank. However we realize that this is not a question of paramount importance. What is vital and necessary is a change of policy so that, first, an increase in our ability to create real wealth should be reflected by an increase in purchasing power; second, goods and services should be distributed to individuals in proportion to the capacity of the nation to produce such goods and services; and third, the control of policy is the most important factor, and our financial policy should be designed to serve industrial and national requirements. I think the right hon. leader of the government (Mr. Mackenzie King) should have no objection to a statement of that kind, because he has said on several occasions that the paramount question is control of policy; that he was not so sure as to the nationalization problem. I think that was referred to as a debatable question. We do not take quite that stand. It may or may not be debatable, but in our estimation that is not the question which is so vitally important. The important question is the control of policy; yet that is one of the points evaded in the resolution. Oh, yes, I know it indicates that some additional directors are to be placed on the board so as to obtain control, but twice in this house I have been told by the leaders of the two great parties that parliament was supreme in every sense of the word. So I ask you, Mr. Chairman, why it is necessary to buy or sell more shares or do anything like that in order to secure control of policy. Why can we not pass legislation here which will give us absolute control? We are not so much concerned with the management of the bank, though we would have no objection whatever if the government thought it necessary to make some change there. That is beside the point. If it is necessary, go ahead

and do it; we would support any measure of that kind. But why in the world can we not, without buying or selling any more shares, pass legislation here in order to obtain complete control of the policy of the bank?
This banking question has been held up as a very mysterious affair, and down through the ages we have been taught to believe that it was something sacred, of which we should not speak at any great length. Another of the theories that have been propounded for many years is that there is and can be only so much sound money. I think everyone is now of the opinion that the so-called sound money theory has been pretty well washed out. Another of the old ideas was that if any more money were created by the government it would be unsound, but that private individuals, private banks, might go ahead and create as much as they saw fit and that would be quite sound. Then, for many years it was considered that the amount of money Canada should have should be regulated by the amount of gold in the country. That was the old gold standard. That theory has now been abandoned, and we believe that the test of the amount of money in circulation should be not only gold but the natural wealth or assets of the country as a whole. If you are going to base money upon something that is necessarily scarce, such as gold, naturally you will have scarce money at all times, and when you leave the issuance of this credit and currency in the care of a few individuals who are solely concerned with the idea of profit, you are bound to have a condition of depression such as we have to-day. So-called depressions are entirely artificial; so are periods of prosperity, because both depressions and periods of prosperity are controlled by the financiers. That is not a question of management; it is a question of the control of policy, and if in this house we devoted our energies more towards securing control of policy I think we would be doing a greater service to the country.
Another old theory, which I think has been well exploded, is that, banks do not create money. They do create it, in every sense of the word. If we had control of policy, and if in this house we considered that the .policy of allowing private individuals to create money should be changed, we could make that change without altering the daily routine of the technical part of banking operations. I believe we are all agreed that the banking industry is very efficiently managed. It is a carefully organized business, and we would not need to interfere at all

Bank oj Canada
with the technique of carrying on that business, All we are concerned with is the question of policy.
I do not wish to take up too much time, but at this point I think it would be well to quote a well known authority for what I have just said. This quotation has been given at other times, but I think it well worth putting on Hansard! again to show that some of these old fallacies are outworn. I quote from the remarks of Right Hon. Reginald McKenna, chairman of the Midland Bank and a former chancellor of the British exchequer, and I do so because he is a recognized banker and financial authority. These are his words:
I am afraid the ordinary citizen will not like to be told that the banks can and do create and destroy money. The amount of money in existence varies only with the action of the banks in increasing or decreasing deposits .. . they who control the credit of a nation direct the policy of governments and hold in the hollow of their hands the destiny of the people.
I contend that such a statement made by a man of the standing of Mr. McKenna should carry a great deal of authority. He says that those who control the credit of a nation direct the policy of government, and that is the point with which we should be concerned. We in this corner believe that the government should take over the control of currency and credit, and until such time as that is done I do not think conditions will greatly improve. The old system is entirely outworn. From the very first it was a debt creating system, and until we change that system we shall have the same conditions existing in this country. As long as we allow these individuals to issue money which starts out as a debt owed by the nation I do not see how we are going to get anywhere. In my opinion money must be issued interest free or at least the necessary amount of money must be issued afterwards to take the place of interest. For instance, if you allow the banks to issue credit to the amount of $100 and at the end of the year 7 per cent interest is charged, that makes a total of $107 which the public is required to pay back. When it is remembered that only $100 was issued to start with can anyone tell me where the $7 interest is to come from?

speechtext:
Now I might refer again to the speech of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler) as reported in Hansard, ait page 453. I will read only a section, as thie bon. leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation referred to this, buit I think it is worth while drawing it to the attention of the committee again:
As the house knows very well, and as I think the country knows, though the people may just as well be reminded of the fact for fear of misrepresentation afterwards-
That is why I am reading it again:
-we on this side of the house were last year almost entirely in favour of a publicly owned central bank. ...
Now there cannot be any doubt of that. I think the minister was quite right when he expressed that opinion. Surely that is what the people expected, and that is what some hon. members expected. The statement I have quoted shows that one of the ministers expected it. We had on this side another Liberal expecting it, when he said the other day, as reported in Hansard, that that was one of the main things he considered they were coming to Ottawa for. I believe, in all sincerity, the people are looking to the government to-day not to do that thing partly, not to take a small step in that direction, but to go ahead and do it as it should be done. If this is to be a publicly owned bank operated in the interests of the people one of the essentials is to cut out interest entirely.

If you wish to add something for overhead, with some technical means of recovering it, there would be no objection to that. That would be a nationally owned bank, in keeping with the election promises.
Another principle of a nationally owned bank would be that money should be issued on the real wealth of the people, instead of allowing a privately organized company, such as the chartered banks or the central bank, to issue money on their own behalf. One of the great evils in our financial system is allowing these individuals or corporations to monetize the real wealth of the people and create an utterly impossible situation for them to meet.
Another essential for a nationally owned bank is that as real wealth increases money should increase. It seems to me to be obvious that as wealth increases money should increase, but during the regime of privately owned banks the system has worked in just the opposite way; as wealth increased they feared for their loans, so they began to call in these loans and thus created the so-called depression. Money should increase as wealth increases; there should be a balanced equation there; purchasing power should at all times equal production, and until that situation is brought about I cannot see that we are going to get very far. Another point for a nationally owned bank is the absolute control of policy by legislation, not merely by buying shares. That seems to me to be paramount.
Now, may rve consider for a moment what the advantages would be to the people of Canada by having a publicly controlled or national central bank. One of the first things that would occur is that it would restore the sovereignty over money to its rightful possessors, namely the people of Canada, through parliament. That is where the control of money should be. This would ensure the lastingness of political freedom. It would make possible the attainment of a just annual living wage for the worker and production at a profit for the farmer. That could be easily done with a properly nationalized bank. Confiscation of the honestly acquired property and savings of the people could be prevented, which is not the case under the present system. I think of some of the farmers, not only in Alberta, but in Ontario and all over the dominion, who toiled sixteen hours a day to get together a little bit of property and then were forced to lose it. As I say, properly constituted policy would prevent confiscation of the honestly acquired property and savings of the people. Again, it would ensure lasting peace among the nations, whose governments would be able' to legislate independently of

Bank oj Canada
the intervention of money changers. The next thing it would do would be to make possible the real freedom of the press and the teaching of the truth in all schools, freed once and for all from the domination of the creators of money; and to ensure independence for industry, which to-day is dominated by finance. That would be one of the great boons. It would also rectify conditions for those who are finding themselves in difficulty in the primary industries. It would ensure equitable credit for all manufacturers who are willing to pay a just living wage for the production of good products, enabling every manufacturer to pay a just living wage annually, free from the competition necessitated by the private control of money. It would eliminate the existence of non-productive bonds, such as victory bonds, which originated in the borrowing of money for digging shell holes and killing soldiers. Money would be backed by real wealth, and, as I suggested a moment ago, as wealth increases so should money, and as wealth decreases so should money, but things which are not productive should not have an earning power.
I think one of the most important features is that it would lessen the burden of taxation. We hear cries everywhere about the increasing burden of taxation, mostly needed for the purpose of taking care of the interest on debt in one form or another, or to carry on public works or to provide pensions for the blind and so on. This would be eliminated to a great degree. It would devise suitable means to distribute purchasing power into the hands of the consumer. You may call that a national dividend, or anything else you wish; it might be put out in that form or another, but sooner or later we are bound to come to that.
If these suggestions are helpful and are carried out the result would mean absolute control of policy; you would not need ownership in any sense of the word but you would have control of policy.
Now hon. members might say that this cannot be done. Again I say that, because it already has been done to some extent, it could be done here in this country. I have before me an article under date of April 3, from a New Zealand newspaper. It reads as follows:
_ The labour government of New Zealand introduced Thursday in the house of representatives a new reserve bank bill, providing for elimination of state capital and the transfer of the bank into an entirely state concern.
The bill also provided for alterations in the machinery of the bank designed to make it more useful. Placing the bank under full state control was a platform of the labour government elected last November.
Shareholders will receive the full market value of their shares, plus an accrued dividend of five shillings (about $1.20) a share.
The bank will regulate and control credit and currency in New Zealand, transfer moneys to or from the island and control the disposal of moneys derived from the sale of any New Zealand products and which for the time being are held overseas.
If New Zealand can do that, why can we not do it? There seems to be no logical reason why we should not do that very thing. The Liberal government, if it did that, would be fulfilling only that which it promised to do for the people of Canada. I say that because I am positive people in this country are expecting the Liberal party to carry out their promises. No longer ago than this morning I received through the mail some editorial comments in The Saskatchewan Liberal of May 28, and from it I shall quote a few lines to show what the people are still expecting.
In view of the disappointment manifest-
As I would like hon. members to take note of the observation, I shall repeat it:
In view of the disappointment manifest in Liberal ranks in Saskatchewan over the decision of the King government not to eliminate private shareholders from the Bank of Canada, but instead, to take control of the bank by the issue of new majority stock to he owned by the government, it is of special interest to note that the new labour government of New Zealand is following the other plan of buying out the shareholders,-the plan which was thought by the rank and file would be followed in Canada.

The present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler) said it in 1935. Why not do it at once; why spread it over a number of years?
A moment ago I said that hon. members in this section of the house would have no objection to one hundred per cent nationalization of the central bank, and in that stand we are in accord with the majority of hon. members in the chamber, including Liberals. I believe that is the opinion they hold. To show what people in Canada and the majority of hon. members expect, may I quote from the report of the banking and commerce committee of March 6, 1934. These are the observations of Mr. Irvine who was a member of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group in the last parliament.
I am quite in agreement with you there, that the bank should be government controlled in all instances.
That is the statement of a man from the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. I want to say that every party would support a policy of this kind.
But the mere ownership by the government of a banking institution or any institution whatsoever will not in itself effect the cure we desire, that is my point.
I want the difference in policy, not a matter of administration, because all that we are doing

Bank oj Canada
if we go from a private corporation to the public, we have only altered the method of administration, we have not altered the policy, and what I want to get at is the essential difference in policy between what you propose and what is now being done.
I think that is what we are all concerned with. The hon. member for Vancouver-Bur-rard (Mr. McGeer), appearing before the banking and commerce committee in 1934, said, as reported at page 703 of the evidence:
1 would not socialize your banks or take away your right to carry on a merchant banking business, if you .wanted to.
There we have a Liberal member emphasizing the control of policy. I believe it was the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) who said the other day, and very justly, when the subject of nationalization was up, that the government could not go into business, and I think he was right. Why change that attitude now? What we desire is an absolute control of policy.
I should like to give one more quotation so as to make the position of the social credit party quite clear and to show that there would be no objection to doing anything of this nature. Major Douglas, speaking before the same banking and commerce committee, said:
So far as I have views, I am all in favour of letting the existing banks run the business. What is fundamentally at stake is the assumption that this monetization which the banks do undoubtedly carry on-the creation of purchasing power-is a creation of purchasing power in their own favour solely, and, as I see it, they do not want to turn it over to the government or hand it over to the public except on their own terms. The result of that assumption and that state of affairs is, that quite beyond all discussion, the assumption is made that all production belongs to the banks since they alone create the effective demand which will cause that production to be delivered, and they claim the ownership of the effective demand which they create.
As I look over the resolution once more, I see that it provides that certain shares shall be purchased by the Minister of Finance out of consolidated revenue fund in order to secure ownership of a majority of the shares by the government, and there is also to be an increase in the number of directors. I could not help wondering just what was in the minds of the government, if it was not to create a few more soft jobs for some people because if the banking business is not being run efficiently I do not know what business is. So far as management is concerned, banking is, beyond comparison, the most efficient business. Why, then, do we want to interfere with it? Why do we want more directors and to 3pend more public money?

As I understand it, the chairman said that he would have to consider the matter, and therefore I assume he is quite prepared to listen to argument before ruling.	I was going to
raise the point that the amendment is contrary to section 54 of the British North America Act, which reads as follows:
It shall not be lawful for the House of Commons to adopt or pass any vote, resolution, address or bill for the appropriation of any part of the public revenue, or of any tax or impost, to any purpose that has not been first recommended to that house by a message of the governor general in the session in which such vote, resolution, address, or bill is proposed.
I draw attention to the words: not lawful for the House of Commons to pass any resolution for the appropriation of any revenue-I quote:
to any purpose that has not been first recommended to that house by a message of the governor general.
The house has before it a resolution of the Minister of Finance, a minister of the crown who preceded his resolution by a recommendation from His Excellency the Governor General, that a measure be introduced to ensure ownership of a majority of the shares of the Bank of Canada by the government. The purpose of the measure is
32S0
Bank of Canada

not, as the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lawson) pointed out a few moments igo, to acquire all the shares, which would amount to complete government ownership. That was the exception taken by the hon. member to the resolution.
My hon. friend's amendment is that the resolution should be amended to provide that all shares of the Bank of Canada shall be purchased by the Minister of Finance. Quite a different purpose. To be in order the amendment would have to be introduced in the house in the first instance in the form of a resolution by a minister of the crown and be recommended to the house by His Excellency the Governor General. May I dlnaw attention to what May says, at page 461:
The committee is not bound by the terms of the provisions which the ministers of the crown have inserted in the bill; and any member may propose to increase the grants specified in these clauses or to extend the application of the provisions of the bill, whatever may be the cost resulting therefrom, so long as the power conferred by the royal recommendation is not exceeded.
The question whether an additional expenditure is involved or not is not the point at issue in this case. It is a question whether the power conferred by the royal recommendation is being exceeded, and all that the royal recommendation has granted, as the hon. member for York South has pointed out, is power to purchase a majority of the shares, but not power to purchase all the shares. The hon. member's amendment is to purchase all the shares.
May I also cite May, 13th edition, at page 546:
An amendment proposing to substitute for the resolution an argumentative justification for the refusal of that demand is out of order, as are also amendments proposed with a view to submitting an alternative scheme to that proposed with the royal recommendation.
The criticism of the government by those who are opposing this resolution as worded is that we have not adopted the alternative scheme which is being proposed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth). Inasmuch as the amendment proposes an alternative scheme, I submit, Mr. Chairman, that it is out of order.

Mr. Chairman, at six o'clock the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) was discussing whether or not the amendment moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) was in order, and apparently you had made up your mind that you were going to give a ruling at eight o'clock. I hope that your mind is not as yet made up. The Prime Minister tried to point out that the amendment was out of order because it conflicted with the recommendations made by the governor in council. I would point out that if that interpretation is to be placed upon the rules of the house, an amendment moved by any hon. member to any bill could be in order. Every amendment to a measure proposed by the government would always be ruled out of order on that ground alone. If your mind is not made up, Mr. Chairman, I should like you to look at paragraph 558 and 559 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, and apply those to the resolution of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning). Paragraph 558 reads:
Motions advocating public expenditure, or the imposition of a charge, if the motion be framed in sufficiently abstract or general terms, can be entertained and agreed to by the house. Resolutions of this nature are permissible because, having no operative effect, no grant is made or burthen imposed by their adoption.
Paragraph 559 reads:
The constitutional principle which vests in the crown the sole responsibility of incurring national expenditure, forbids an increase by the commons of a sum demanded on behalf of the crown for the service of the state. This principle, however, is apparently disregarded when the recommendation of the crown is given to a resolution empowering the expenditure of public money which, framed in general terms, places no limitation on the amount of expenditure to be authorized by the resolution.
I claim that the resolution moved by the Minister of Finance does not state any specific amount. The resolution, reads:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to amend the Bank of Canada Act so as to increase the capital stock of the bank, to provide that certain shares thereof shall be purchased by the Minister of Finance out of the consolidated revenue fund in order to assure ownership of a majority of the shares by the government, to increase the number of directors, and to provide for election and appointment of directors in such manner as to assure voting control of the board by directors appointed by the government.
I claim that the amendment is exactly in accordance with paragraphs 558 and 559. May I go a little further than that? In the first

Bank oj Canada
place there is no actual increased expenditure implied by the amendment of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. In fact, I would argue that actually it means a decrease. The government proposes an expenditure that would be equivalent to the value of about fifty-one per cent of the stock owned by the private shareholders of the present Bank of Canada. My hon. friend suggests that instead of the government taking funds and applying them to the purchase of new shares to number more than the total owned by private investors in the bank, these funds should be utilized for the purpose of buying up what would ultimately be the minority of the shareholders of the bank. In that way I claim the amendment actually means a decrease and not an increase in the expenditure proposed. Second, the amendment moved by my hon. friend is in exact conformity with paragraphs 558 and 559, and I respectfully submit that the amendment is absolutely in order.

Mr. Chairman, I should like ho direct a, few remarks to the Prime Minis,ter (Mr. Mackenzie King). I merely wish ,to say that if this amendimenit is ruled out of order because of the reasons given by the Prime Minister in his observations prior to six o'clock, a precedent will be laid down that no member shall be permitted to suggest any amendment to or interfere in any way with a resolution introduced by the government and preceding a bill. If such a decision is made, I submit that it will be extremely serious. I appreciate the point raised by the Prime Minister, but I still believe it is covered by the rules. In addition to the paragraphs cited by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Heaps) I think attention should be directed to paragraph 555 of Beauchesne's Rules and Forms, which reads:
No increase can be considered either of an existing, or of a new or temporary tax for the service of the year, except on the initiative of a minister acting on behalf of the crown.
Of course, that is a well known and well accepted rule. I now direct attention to paragraph 556, which reads:
The house can make amendments which dimmish the amount of reduction of taxation, or postpone the day when the reduction takes place, although the amendment may increase to that extent the charges proposed to be levied upon the people.
It may be argued that those rules refer to taxation, but after all the principle involved is this: It is not competent for a private member to introduce a measure which imposes a charge upon the public revenue. That
is the broad principle. It does not matter whether that principle is applicable to estimates or to a bill of a specific kind involving the expenditure of public money. It may be argued-and I think this is the point raised by the Prime Minister-that inasmuch as this is a resolution preceding a bill introduced by the government, therefore it is not competent for a private member to move an amendment. But estimates are also resolutions submitted to His Excellency the Governor General in exactly the same way as was this resolution. Having received his approval, they are offered to the house for its approval. Although such a measure contains the express view of the government and has been submitted to His Excellency the Governor General, under the rules the house may make amendments as long as they do not offer or purport to increase the amount.
In this instance the resolution has been submitted in very general terms, as has been indicated by the hon. member for Winnipeg North. The terms are broad; no specific amount is mentioned, nor is the exact manner in which the shares are to be acquired stated; the resolution simply says that it is expedient to bring in a measure so as to increase capital stock of the bank, to provide that certain shares thereof-it does not say what shares-shall be purchased by the Minister of Finance. I submit that the minister could very well argue, when this resolution and the bill to be founded upon it are passed, that he is empowered to buy all the shares of the Bank of Canada, the new issue and the old issue, if he so desires. Those being the general powers of the resolution, I do not see that an amendment suggesting a slight modification and limitation of the original motion should be regarded as out of order and not competent for a private member to move.
The Prime Minister has always been, very properly, a great champion of the rights of individual members of the house. I appeal to him that, before it is asked that this amend-nent should be ruled out of order, careful consideration should be given to the possible jffect in the future of a precedent of this kind. I know he does not wish to lay down a rule of principle or practice that would curb the rights of private members. There have been occasions before in this session and previous ones when I have noticed the government taking an attitude towards members' amendments which I felt was probably unwarranted, and restrictive of what I believe to be the rights of private members. That is the feature I wish to emphasize, and while it would be most distasteful to me to differ from or challenge a ruling of the chair, I strongly
Bank of Canada

urge a reconsideration of this matter and that, in view of the desire of, I think, every one in this house to preserve the rights of private members, this amendment be permitted.

My contention is that the government cannot be chastised for something and at the same time be expected to support the very thing for which chastisement is being administered. My hon. friend the member for York South (Mr. Lawson), who this afternoon is apparently acting as financial critic on behalf of the opposition, directed his criticism against the Minister of Finance on the score that this resolution was not a resolution for complete government ownership of the bank. He said that, therefore, we were not implementing the pledges we made in the general election. Had I spoken immediately following my hon. friend, I would have thanked him for having made clear to the house-and I should like to do so now, and thank as well my hon. friend the member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) and other hon. members-for having brought out so clearly the entire consistency of the course which was followed by myself in the statements I made in the recent campaign and previously in the House of Commons with regard to the government's policy and position on this matter of a properly constituted Central National Bank.

That is very
decidedly the point the Prime Minister makes; that is one of his main points, and in any ruling that may be given by the chair I think that point should be answered.
The Prime Minister's main objection is that this alternative motion has not the recommendation of the governor general. May I point out what it would really amount to if this were declared out of order. Based upon this resolution a bill will be brought into the house. That bill must be founded upon this resolution; as I understand it the
