principle of the bill cannot be different from the principle of the resolution. It must be exactly the same, otherwise we would be disregarding the governor general; once we got the resolution through we would be introducing another idea altogether, another proposal. So if to-day it is ruled that we cannot introduce an amendment to the resolution it means that we cannot introduce an amendment to the bill, which would reduce this house to a nullity, a mere debating society.
That is a stronger position than was taken by the previous government in connection with the original bill setting up the Bank of Canada. Some of the older members will recall that we on this side-and I am still on the side I was on in those days-attempted to introduce an amendment on second reading. The Speaker of that time would not permit us to do so. I quote from page 4374 of Hansard of 1934:
Mr. Rhodes: That is the only principle. The point whether this bank should he publicly or privately owned as well as questions respecting the numerous other details incidental to the bill are matters of detail which can be dealt with by way of amendment in the regular course as we proceed in committee on banking and commerce, or in committee of the whole house, or upon motion on the third reading of the bill.
Notwithstanding this, when the third reading of the bill did come, we were prohibited from introducing any amendment. The Liberals, who were then in opposition, also tried to introduce an amendment, but we were both ruled out of order. That meant that we could not introduce any change on the second reading or on the third reading, and I submit that if the government presses this matter and upholds the principle that we cannot introduce an amendment of this kind it completely rules out the possibility of this house really having control of legislation. The Prime Minister emphasized the need of the government being consulted in this matter, and so on. Well, I can remember back in 1925 when the Prime Minister took the ground very strongly that the governor general could not interfere in any way with the decision of his ministers; that the decision of the ministers ought to be final. The Prime Minister took a strong stand on that occasion in connection with the position of the governor general. Now it would seem that he is switching round completely and saying that until the governor general consents to every detail of money legislation, this house is helpless. That is an impossible situation. Surely this parliament has rights, just as much as in those days the government had rights. I

supported the government in those days; little did I think the time would come when that very government, appealing for support because of its Liberal principles, would attempt to deprive parliament of its right to control legislation. I protest against any decision which would take away those rights and powers.

When my hon. friend speaks of depriving parliament of the rights it has in connection with legislation I hope he will not dispute that these rights are set out within the four corners of the British North America Act. At the moment I should like to direct the attention of the committee to one of the provisions of the British North America Act which is most specific with regard to matters of legislation. It is section 54 of the British North America Act, which reads as follows:
It shall not be lawful for the House of Commons to adopt or pass any vote, resolution, address, or bill for the appropriation of any part of the public revenue, or of any tax or impost, to any purpose that has not been first recommended to that house by message of the governor general in the session in which such vote, resolution, address, or bill is proposed.
That is the situation. There has been no recommendation presented to this house by any minister of the crown carrying the recommendation of His Excellency the Governor General, in accordance with the terms of the constitution, which ask powers for the government to acquire all shares in order to obtain complete ownership of the Bank of Canada. There having been no such request made on the intiative of any minister of the crown on the recommendation of the governor general, I submit that it is impossible lawfully so to pass the resolution. The power requested by the resolution is less than that which is asked for by the amendment, and the bill is one pertaining to public expenditure.

... if the motion be framed in sufficiently abstract or general terms, can be entertained, and agreed to by the house. Resolutions of this nature are permissible because, having no operative effect, no grant is made or burthen imposed by their adoption.

The Prime Minister has invoked an argument which I was about to apply to himself. He says those who do not like this motion can vote against it. That is precisely what can be done with the amendment. What the Prime Minister is doing is confusing his rights and powers as a government with a majority to vote on something that is proposed with the right of a private member to introduce any amendment to such a resolution. Let me draw the attention of the committee to section 54 of the British North America Act:
It shall not be lawful for the House of Commons to adopt or pass any vote, resolution, address, or bill for the appropriation of any part of the public revenue, or of any tax or impost, to any purpose that has not been first recommended to that house by message of the governor general. . . .
What does that mean? It means that this house cannot on its own initiative pass an appropriation of the public revenue. That has nothing at all to do with the question before us; it is not the point at issue. The point at issue is: Can this house, having received at the hands of the government a certain motion which has been submitted to His Excellency the Governor General, consider that motion and, if it deems it advisable, amend it? I submit that the adoption of the view of the Prime Minister would establish a precedent which would seriously curb the rights of hon. members and limit the usefulness of the House of Commons in the
consideration of legislation. Section 54 of the British North America is not applicable to this instance at all.
I simply content myself with pointing this out, because certainly the question will have to come to an issue some day. This may not be a sufficiently important matter on which to bring it to an issue, but sooner or later the issue is bound to rise: Shall the members of this house, as members, have rights or shall they not? I warn the Prime Minister that the course he is pursuing amounts to this, that if a government, it does not matter what government, chooses to come to the house with a certain proposal, they can say, that is our proposal, we will not entertain any suggestions in regard to it. That would be a very dangerous precedent to establish.

I may say to hon.
members of the committee that since the committee rose at six o'clock I have given the amendment of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) very careful attention, and I have also listened attentively to the arguments advanced by all hon. members who have spoken since eight o'clock.
This is not a motion for appropriation of public moneys. It is a proposed resolution under standing order 60 for a charge upon the people to be voted upon another occasion and it is required in order that a bill to amend the Bank of Canada Act, a bill involving an expenditure, be introduced. The 'fundamental terms of the resolution submitted to the house with the governor general's recommendation, upon which this committee was appointed, cannot be amended. Amendments will be in order only if they fall within the terms of the resolution. May, 13th edition, page 546, says that the procedure in committees on money resolutions follows in principle the procedure of the committee of supply, and that amendments are out of order if they are proposed with a view to substituting an alternative scheme to that proposed with the royal recommendation. The point was decided by Mr. Whitley, then chairman of committees in the British House of Commons, on October 22, 1917. I therefore rule that the amendment is out of order.

Speaking to the main motion, I have already stated, Mr. Chairman, that we were not opposing the complete nationalization of the Bank of Canada, but rather that we were more in favour of complete government control, and judging by the Prime Minister's remarks a little while ago he also is in favour of that idea. The main point, so far as the Bank of Canada is concerned, is that we should have control. The means to be taken to secure that control is another question. The government proposes to issue enough new stock to get control. We contend that that is not necessary; that the government could get control outright by legislation. Control is the predominating question, and on this question that control is an essential factor I should like to quote from an authority, Reverend Charles E. Coughlin, to show how the central bank could control all other phases of banking. He has published a little book entitled Money, which deals with the subject in the form of question and answer, and while it has reference to the federal government in the United States it should be applicable to the federal government in this country. The first question is this:
1.	Who should own all the local banks?
The answer to that is:
Local banks should be owned by privately owned corporations chartered by the respective states wherein they are located. The federal government should coin and regulate all money, but private banks should lend money owned by private citizens.
That brings out clearly that control should lie with the central bank, and that control can be secured by legislation. The next question is this:
2. Should these banks just described be controlled in any manner by the government?
That again brings up the question of government control. The answer to that question is:
Since these privately owned banks are state chartered, they should be controlled by the state.
For "state" read "dominion government." It goes on:
It should be the duty of the state government to set up equitable rules and regulations under which these banks must operate.
Bank of Canada

That is the point I wish to emphasize, that we in this parliament should secure control by means of legislation without the necessity of owning a single share. The next question is this:
3.	With what kind of money would the banks do business?
The answer to that is:
These banks would do business only with United States-
Read "Canadian" for "United States":
-legal tender which private individuals or corporations actually brought to the banks.
I should now like to quote from a little pamphlet which I was amused to pick up in one of the banks the other day, and which is entitled, The Public and The Ranks, by James Muir. It deals with some of the misleading ideas that are being broadcast to-day. It says:
You may be interested to learn that the banks operate nearly five million deposit accounts in Canada. Surely, when so much confidence has been shown in us, it is absolutely essential and obligatory that the banks should be keenly aware of their duties to these millions of people. All of which means that banks must be kept at all times in condition to meet, at a moment's notice, a depositor's request for his money.

I may say that my conception to-day is quite different from what it was when I first came to Ottawa, and it is changing all the time. I do not suppose I had better refer to that pamphlet again because apparently it is mostly all wrong. What I was trying to show by quoting from that pamphlet was how banking could be controlled entirely through legislation. All these misrepresentations that are being circulated could be rectified right here in this house.
I want to refer again to this resolution and the control of policy. During the election we heard a great cry about the wonderful monetaiy reforms which were to be brought about, how it was going to benefit the people if they voted Liberal and got these monetary reforms. As I pointed out a little while ago. one of the essential features of a nationally owned bank should be the reduction, or perhaps the complete elimination of interest rates. Not long ago I listened to some remarks by the hon. member for Jasper-Edson (Mr. Ivuhl), and I should like to refer again to them. The hon. member was speaking about the principle which should be laid down by the government in this banking measure. He is reported at page 1835 of Hansard of April 6, as follows:
Mr. Kuhl: May I ask the Prime Minister a question? Is it necessary for the dominion government to go into debt for any public works projects, no matter Lo what extent?

Mr. Kuhl: Is it necessary?

I think that is one of the main principles which should be brought down in legislation. The government is going to get control by the purchase of additional shares; yet I doubt if there is to be any material change in policy. According to the Prime Minister, there would seem to be some truth in the rumour that we are still to borrow money from, I assume, the banks and go still further into debt. I tried to point out a while ago that the purpose of a nationally owned bank should be to reduce debt expenditures and thereby reduce taxation. It seems to me more evident as I go along that the point we should stress in parliament, as the Prime Minister said a moment ago, is a change of policy, and that policy should be brought down right now. As I look over the resolution I cannot see that by the proposed change the central bank is going to be anything more than a privately owned bank. We are to have the government in business, holding a majority of the shares. That is true enough; yet all the other obligations of this 49 per cent of shareholders will have to be met. It will be just a privately owned bank, with the government as one of the shareholders. The other 49 per cent must be paid their dividend according to the act, and the interest must be paid. The measure still permits, to a degree at least, the monetization of the real wealth of the people rather than having it controlled entirely by the government. One thing I notice is lacking. I may be called out of order for making this observation; nevertheless it seems to me to be in order; and it is, that in this Bank of Canada Act there is no mention whatever of the control of the chartered banks. I think one of the evils which required attention lay in the conduct of the chartered banks; there should be some control of them, and it should be provided for at once.
As I have said, one of the promises made by the Liberals during the election was a monetary change, and if I may be permitted to refer to Hansard, ait page 1982, I will show the committee exactly what the people expected. It is contained in the speech of a Liberal who, I see, is not in his place to-day, but from whom I expected to hear a great deal on the bank question, because I listened to him on the platform in Alberta, and I expected that as a Liberal he would take a

I should like hon. members to note that.
-I thought we came here to take over from the Bank of Canada the industry of manufacturing Canadian capital. I want to go further and say that until such time as we are prepared to vest in the government of this dominion the power to create, issue and regulate currency and credit in terms of public need, there will be no solution of either the tax, the debt or the unemployment problems in the Dominion of Canada.
Unless Liberals take heed to some of the suggestions that have been given them to-day and carry out some of the election promises they made all over the dominion not long ago, they are surely building a cross upon which they themselves will 'be crucified at the next election, if not before.

Personally I am not very much concerned whether the Bank of Canada Act is amended or not. I do not think it requires amendment to enable the government and parliament to make very wide and extensive use of the powers of the present Bank of Canada as set forth in the existing statute. What is of importance, I believe, to this country is: what is the purpose behind it all? What is the intention of the government? What is this policy that is to be put into operation after the Bank of Canada Act has been amended? A few moments ago, when we were discussing the point of order, I read a section of the preamble of the act. Perhaps I might repeat

that, merely to emphasize what I desire to request of the minister. The preamble of the existing act declares that the purpose of the act is, among other things:

to control and protect the external value of the national monetary unit and to mitigate by its influence fluctuations in the general level of production, trade, prices and employment, so far as may be possible within the scope of monetary action, and generaly to promote the economic and financial welfare of the dominion.
That is an indication of the purpose of the creation of the Bank of Canada. It will still remain, I assume, as the general declaration of the purpose of the bank. I should like to ask the minister whether on the second reading of the bill to be founded upon this resolution he would be good enough to make a statement of the policy of the government, having in mind these broad declarations of intention as to the use of this bank, and having also in mind the needs of the country at the present time. One other request I make of the minister is this: Would he delay the second reading for, say three days to give us an opportunity to read the printed bill and give it a reasonable amount of study? I suggest this because the bill amending the Bank of Canada Act is, in my opinion, the most important piece of legislation suggested to the house this session, and it is not unreasonable, I think, to ask that we be given two or three days to study a bill which we have not yet seen.
While I am on my feet, and just to complete my observations, may I say that the minister, in presenting his resolution, made an excellent resume of the functions of central banks, and the history of them in various countries. Mr. TUCKER; The reason I referred to it was that I took it that the hon. member for Kootenay East quoted it with approval, and as far as I am concerned I want to repudiate it on behalf of the Liberal party, in so far as I may speak in a humble way for that party. Like the hon. member who has just spoken, I consider that the measure before the house is one of the most important that has come before parliament at this session. Like him I agree that it should be the wish and the will of this parliament to give all the time necessary to the discussion of this very important question.
It seems to me that as far as the Liberal party is concerned we take the attitude that we have, as it were, two main lines of attack on our present problems. The first is to lower the obstacles to trade in order that Canada may exchange her surplus products, of which she has no need, for the surplus pioducts of other lands in order to increase the total amount of wealth available for distribution among the Canadian people. That is the primary policy of the Liberal parly, the policy of freer trade among the nations of the world. The second line of attack has become increasingly important. It was enunciated by the leader of the Liberal party, the present Prime Minister, in this Hou-e of Commons on February 27, 1933, as follows:
The Liberal party recognizes that the problem of distribution has become more important than that of production. It believes that personality is more sacred than property. In all its policies it has been guided by that principle, above everything else. It will continue to devote itself to finding ways and means of effecting a fair and just distribution of wealth with increasing regard to human need, to the furtherance of social justice and to the promotion of the common good.

As far as I am concerned, I consider that we have come to the point, in the words of that statement of policy, where the problem of the production of wealth within the country and its exchange with other countries is not as important as the problem of the distribution of that wealth among the people of Canada. So I take this attitude: We have spent many days on the very important problem of lowering the tariffs in order to increase the wealth available for distribution among our people, and we should be willing to go in great detail into what I regard as the first great approach to the problem of a more equitable distribution of our wealth among our people. I may be wrong, but as I see it this is the first important legislation to be brought down designed to make a definite attack upon that problem of the distribution of wealth. I think this government has gone very far, in its first session, in carrying out its promise to lower the tariff. In my opinion in this bill the government is going a considerable distance toward monetary reform.
Some hon. members who have spoken previously have suggested that this legislation does not go the full length of one hundred per cent ownership and control of the Bank of Canada. As far as I am concerned, if it were a question of government ownership or government control I should say that the important thing was government control. That is the all important thing, because, after all, when you consider the question of ownership you have at the same time to consider certain incidental rights. If you cut down those rights to the point where mere legal ownership carries no rights whatever, then your ownership practically vanishes, and it seems to me that as far as the shareholders of the Bank of Canada are concerned in all respects but one we are approaching that point. We are saying to them: "We will leave you the possession and ownership of your shares but we will take away from you the right to control the policy of the institution. We vest that right in a brand new set of people of whom you had no knowledge when you invested in those shares, and they can, if they wish, guide and direct the destinies of that institution without regard to your wishes. The only right we leave with you is the right to draw 4J per cent per year in dividends if, under the guidance and control of that new body, the bank manages to earn such dividends." Therefore I submit, Mr. Chairman, that in effect we have taken over one hundred per cent control of this institution. We are taking actual ownership to the extent of fifty-one
Bank of Canada

per cent, and by virtue of taking over complete control we have deprived the people who still retain the technical ownership of their shares, of most of the rights incidental to such ownership. So I take it that we have proceeded, to the extent of somewhere between seventy-five per cent and one hundred per cent, to assume complete ownership of the Bank of Canada.
As far as I am concerned I should like to make it clear that if in the first session of this parliament, having this bill before us with the ability to pass it through this house, hoping and expecting that it will go through both houses of parliament, we can proceed from seventy-five per cent to one hundred per cent along the road to complete ownership and control of the central bank, it seems to me that is something worth while, which should receive enthusiastic support in this house and throughout the country. I do not suggest that I would not have liked to see this bill provide for the government taking over every share owned by private interests. Personally I would have been gratified to have seen that, but I am not one of those who, because they cannot get their own way entirely, will not go seventy-five per cent of the way, which at the moment is as far as my fellows in the same party are prepared to go. After all, the only person in any country in the world, under any system of government, who can get his own way at all times is a man like Mussolini, and we want no Mussolinis in Canada. I do not fancy that any single member of parliament thinks he should have the rights that Mussolini has.
I should like to suggest to the Minister of Finance, however, that one of the rights we do leave these shareholders is the right to draw 4i per cent on the money they have invested, and incidentally we have practically guaranteed that dividend. The hon. member for York South (Mr. Lawson) the leading financial critic of the opposition, suggested that when the gold was turned over to the Bank of Canada good value was given for it. I suggest that such was not the case, and that by virtue of that little deal the previous government absolutely guaranteed those shareholders earnings several times in excess of the dividend they are supposed to get. What did the government do? They turned over to that bank $69,000,000 of gold, in round figures, and $986,000 of silver, and they provided that for every dollar of gold held by the Bank of Canada it could issue $4 in printed paper money. So. by turning over to that bank $69,000,000 in gold, we put it within the power of that institution to print, in round figures, $277,821,000 of paper money, which we declared to be legal tender. But, the last

government said, because the Bank of Canada has to redeem $185,000,000 worth of Dominion of Canada notes, in addition to the gold which we have given it, we are going to give it $115,000,000 in government bonds, bearing interest at 3 per cent, carrying an annual income of $3,450,000, payable in cash in 1940. In order, forsooth, that the Bank of Canada can redeem $185,000,000 worth of dominion government notes we have given them gold whereby they can issue legal tender to almost $100,000 000 more (than the amount they have to redeem); yet we have to give them our bonds on top of that. What kind of sound finance is that? It is costing the people of this country, by virtue of setting up the Bank of Canada, $3,450,000 annually until 1940, an out and out gift to the Bank of Canada, and we are going to hand them the money, $115,000,000, in 1940. There is the situation. By what manner of means can that be justified? If you went to the Bank of Canada to-day with a dominion government note and said: Under the Bank of Canada Act you must redeem that note; you have already been paid for it; what would they give you? They would give you another note, printed by themselves, issued against the gold they have already received from the government. And because they do that they are actually going to be paid $115,000,000 in 1940 and in the meantime be paid $3,450,000 annually. That means that we have guaranteed the Bank of Canada -they cannot possibly lose that much surely- an income of four and a half per cent to these people who have invested in that stock.
There are two points I suggest in regard to that. The first is that in my humble judgment the time has come that this dominion should not pay a bit more than one per cent for its money. And we should not perpetuate the condition of anybody drawing four and a half per cent as a result of government operations in finance. Some people who invested in Bank of Canada stock may take the attitude that the government should not cut down their rate of interest. In view of the fact that the banks to-day are paying depositors only one and a half per cent, when they formerly paid three per cent, if the banks have the right to cut down the rate of interest to the extent of fifty per cent, I suggest that we should cut down the rate of dividend payable on these shares to at least the same rate which the banks pay to their depositors. Then I would say to these shareholders: If any of you are not satisfied with one and a half per cent, we will take your shares over at the actual market value. I make that suggestion to the Minister of Finance as a fair and equitable arrangement. It is not a fair or equitable arrange-

Well, I sought to show

If we actually pay the Bank of Canada $3,450,000 annually until 1940 and at that time actually hand over to them $115,000,000, having made that donation to these people who only put $5,000,000 into the proposition, if they cannot pay four and a half per cent during our lifetime they are not the clever people they were represented to be. It is a most amazing thing. We pay the Bank of Canada that amount of interest, and I know some people boast about the wonderful success that attended the operation of the Bank of Canada last year. According to their annual report, having drawn from us that amount in interest, they turned over to the receiver general of Canada, $346,000. It is true they transferred $173,000 to rest account. But apparently it took quite a bit to operate the central bank. I suggest that having given them those rights we should have absolute control of that institution.
One reason why I suggest that we should have absolute control of the Bank of Canada is in view of its power over the prices that prevail in the country. It is suggested in the preamble to the Bank of Canada Act that a properly constituted central bank will have an influence on price levels. Some people seem to have the idea that prices are pretty well governed by supply and demand and that monetary action has nothing to do with the level of prices. I suggest that we should take control of the central bank because I think it is very important to operate upon our general price level so that the burden of debt, of interest and of fixed charges in this country will be decreased. In western Canada- and the same is true in eastern Canada, but I speak of western Canada because I know something of conditions there-we have had the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act operating, and I do not think any board has worked harder or more sincerely or more anxiously to try to meet the difficulties of the farming community than the board of review and the different officers operating the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act in Saskatchewan. But what has happened is this- I think I am in order, and perhaps I should justify myself before I am called to order -people went to western Canada, many from the old province of Ontario; they went
out there thirty or forty years ago; they worked and their families worked and they saved. I know some hon. members suggest that the farmers have been extravagant; that they bought a Ford car perhaps, or after twenty years of work took a trip to California. But when a family in western Canada and their children worked and deprived themselves of what they needed for twenty or thirty years, were they not entitled to a cheap car and to possibly one trip away during that time? I submit that is not extravagance. I submit this-and every hon. member knows it is true-that there is no equal number of people on the face of the globe who in the same period of time have produced so much real wealth as the people living in western Canada. But what do we find to-day? We find that the majority of people in western Canada actually owe more than they own.

upwards of prices. That is one of the purposes for which I hope we are taking control of the bank. In connection with the fact that the central bank should operate on the level of prices I shall argue first of all that it is very important that it be government owned and controlled.
I have in my hand the report of the committee on finance and industry, known as the British Macmillan report. Paragraph 31 reads as follows:
It follows that the functions of a central bank and the obligations resting upon it are of a very special character, calling for skill, experience and judgment of a kind different from those which must be possessed by commercial bankers. No banker can neglect the rules of prudence and of safety, but the object of a commercial banker is to make a profit. The situation of the Central Bank is such that it must often undertake operations which are not only not profitable, but result in losses. Its aim must be the safety of the financial system and the economic welfare of the country.
In view of the words in the British Macmillan report I argue that as the central bank must often undertake operations resulting in losses, the less profit interest there is involved which is inevitably concerned with losses on capital investment, the more likely are the best interests of the country to be served, and the less likely it is that too much consideration will be given to the earning of profits.
In connection with the purpose of a central bank I should like first of all to read from the resolutions passed at the imperial conference at Ottawa, and in connection therewith I shall read in the first place from the statement by the present leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), the then Prime Minister, to the conference:
Canada, like all other countries, has suffered severely from the calamitous fall in commodity prices.	Since August. 1929, our index of
wholesale prices has fallen 32 per cent and is now only 4 per cent above the pre-war level. This means that the dollar has increased in purchasing power by 48 per cent. As a result of this rapid and persistent decline in the general price level and the inevitable disparities created between different kinds of prices, normal business relationships have been disrupted. profit margins have disappeared in many cases, enterprise has been discouraged, unemployment has steadily increased, the fiscal problems of all our public bodies have been greatly aggravated, and the burden of fixed charges is exerting an almost intolerable pressure upon some of the strategic elements in our national economy.
Interest charges represent the most important of the fixed or semi-rigid -elements in our cost structure. If prices remain on their present level, such charges will constitute an intolerable or almost intolerable burden in many cases. Even if it can be borne, the fortuitous gain to the creditor of 40 to 48 per cent in general purchasing power above what he contracted for appears to be a grave injustice.
That was the situation as explained by -the then leader of the Canadian delegation at the imperial conference as to the necessity of restoring the level of prices so that the burden of interest, debt and fixed charges would not be intolerable.
I should like to quote from the statement of the Right Hon. S. M. Bruce, leader of the Australian delegation at that conference, and I do so because I think it is very important that this country should be fully seized of the fact that we can by operating through the central bank restore, if we so desire, the level of prices, and in order that the Canadian people may know where to place the blame if the price level is left where it is and the burden of debt in its present intolerable load is left around the necks of our people. I wish to go into this with some considerable degree of care. As I said at the outset, the question of the tariff is important, 'but this question is equally important and the members of this parliament should in my opinion be prepared to give it their serious attention.
In passing, I regret that the right hon. leader of the opposition is not in his seat tonight. Young member as I am of this house I have given some study to the work he did following the Imperial Economic Conference, and particularly what he did along those lines in this country. After this statement was given to the Imperial Economic Conference by the present leader of the opposition, then Prime Minister, we find him coming back from the conference and expanding the actual currency of Canada by $53,000,000. He also put through a transaction whereby treasury bills were discounted with the banks, resulting in $35,000,000 more of currency being put into circulation. In other words, following the economic conference, the Prime Minister of Canada and his government put into circulation over $80,000,000 of new currency, and I submit that had he courageously continued to follow that policy the situation would be different to-day. Prices began to rise; farmers began to get more for their wheat and other products; people in the factories got more for what they had to sell, and business conditions generally were being restored through the placing in circulation of an adequate supply of money. I can show that by giving the rise in the level of prices if I have time. Having taken that action, instead of continuing in it, the then Prime Minister set up a privately owned central bank and gave them control of the situation, and since then, so far as I can see there has been not a thing done in the way of putting out more purchasing power. There has been, on the contrary, deflation, and it is time that we took control of the central bank to reverse that
Bank oj Canada

process. That is the question to which I wish to direct my remarks to-night, and which I submit should engage the attention of this house.
The Right Hon. Stanley Bruce, leader of the Australian delegation, said:
There is no question of greater interest to Australia at the present conference than that of action to bring about a higher price level and stability of exchange. Unless an increase in commodity prices can be achieved it is difficult to see how the present financial and economic system of the world can be maintained. In relation to this conference of British countries it is obvious that any reciprocal tariff arrangements that are arrived at can be of little benefit unless the paralysis of trade is stayed and the price level is raised.
The peoples of the world have shown remarkable patience in submitting to the severe adjustments already made. But they have not been enough. As to the further action needed, one school of thought maintains that the only way out is that we should go on reducing down to the point that will allow profitable production on the basis of the present price level. Another school maintains that it is impossible to bring about the necessary further reductions and that a solution can be found only by an increase in commodity prices and the stabilizing of exchange.
He goes on:
Australia subscribes to the second view.
I could read more as to the action that should be taken in the opinion of Mr. Bruce, but time will not permit.
I wish to quote now from the statement of Hon. N. C. Havenga, leader of the South African delegation:
We are all oppressed by the phenomenally low level of commodity prices. We all desire higher prices, but what we mean is not that cheapness, or in other words, plenty, is an economic evil, but that having made all our dispositions on the level of values of say 1928, we find that all our machinery is out of gear when we have to sell at the prices of 1932.
But must we act on the assumption that this state of affairs will continue indefinitely? What are the great economic factors in the world to-day?
We have plenty of commodities, and the power of producing much more if need be.
We have millions of people desiring those commodities but lacking in an effective demand for them. We have millions of money, seeking safe investment, and unwilling to assume the risk of carrying out its normal function, which is to link up the commodities with the people requiring them.
But we lack the gear-lever which will link up the machinery of production through universal joints to the differential of consumption which will set in motion the wheels of progress.
There Mr. Havenga puts his finger on what I submit our party had in mind when it said that the problem of distribution had become of more importance than that of production. That is a question to which I think every
	*
member of parliament should give the best possible attention.
I have Iquoted Mr. Havenga because nobody would suggest that he was identified with any party in this house. I should also like to quote a sentence or two from the statement of Sir Henry Strakosch, one of the delegates from India:
The fall in prices and the consequent process of economic disintegration has already reached so advanced a stage that there is no time to lose. If we are to avoid troubles far more acute and far more dangerous than those we have already experienced, quick and determined action is necessary.
I should like now to read the resolutions which were adopted at the imperial conference held in Ottawa in 1932. and I do so because they represent the considered judgment of the leading statesmen of the empire. I submit and urge that we should give some consideration to carrying out what these leading statesmen of the empire stated was necessary in order to restore a reasonable measure of economic adjustment for the peoples of the empire. This is from the first resolution:
A rise throughout the world in the general levels of wholesale prices is in the highest degree desirable. The evil of falling prices must be attacked by government and individual action in all its causes whether political, economic, financial or monetary.
There is a definite recommendation. A further resolution states:
In the monetary sphere the primary line of action towards a rise in prices should be the creation and maintenance, within the limits of sound finance, of such conditions as will assist in the revival of enterprise and trade.

Bank of Canada
authorities speak. I should like to direct the attention of the committee to some things which speak more eloquently than I can. I have in my hand the report of the committee on banking and commerce which sat in 1934, and I quote from pages 88 and 89, in connection with the consideration of a motion presented by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) on March 15, as follows:
That before proceeding with the discussion, clause by clause, of Bill No. 19, an act to incorporate the Bank of Canada, the select standing committee on banking and commerce is of opinion that the proposed Bank of Canada should be owned and controlled by the Dominion of Canada and that the provisions of the said bill should be altered accordingly.
Those in favour were:
Messrs. Bothwell, Casgrain, Coote, Donnelly, Duff, Euler, Howard, Lapointe, Mackenzie (Vancouver Centre), Power, Raymond, Sanderson and Spencer.
With the exception of Mr. Spencer and Mr. Coote, the rest were members of the Liberal party, some now being members of the cabinet. The motion which they supported was not only for control; it was that the central bank should be owned and controlled by the Dominion of Canada. I submit that if that was a good motion to make and support in 1934 with a Conservative government in power, it is a good motion to make and support in 1936, with a Liberal government in power. The gentlemen who supported that motion are saying nothing about it to-day. We must either assume that they supported it to embarrass the government of that day, or that they have since changed their minds with reference to the ownership and control of the Bank of Canada.
In Saskatchewan we have heard the opinions of members of the Liberal party as to a central bank. I hold in my hand the report of the Agricultural Credit Commission of that province, appointed in 1913. This report gives a very fine summary of conditions in the province at that time, when they were not good for the agriculturist. Those who signed that report were: J. H. Haslam, Charles A. Dunning and Edmund H. Oliver. After reviewing the conditions which existed, they made some very fine recommendations.

That legislation be enacted to provide for the establishment of a cooperative mortgage association for the raising of funds on mortgage bonds and the granting of loans to farmers on
mortgage security for approved agricultural productive or improvement purposes only; such legislation to embody the features hereinafter mentioned.

That the Saskatchewan Cooperative Farm Mortgage Association establish as soon after its foundation as is feasible a bank with headquarters within the province to conduct a regular banking business both through branches of its own and, wherever possible, with and through the locals, and officers of the association.
As I read that I submit that the Minister of Finance has moved a long way from the position he then held.

I am reminded of the lines of Dorothy Parker, who said:
When I was young and bold and strong, Then right was right and wrong was wrong; With plume on high and flag unfurled I went forth to fight the world.
"Come out and fight, you dogs," said I,
And wept there was but once to die.
Now I am old, and good and bad Are woven in a crazy plaid.
I sit and say "The world is so And he is wise who lets it go.
A victory lost a victory won
The difference is so small, my son."
Thus inertia rides and riddles me,
The which is called philosophy.
An hon. gentleman opposite said that I should speak for myself, but I should like to give the stand of the Liberal party on this question. I have before me some of the campaign literature which was circulated in my constituency. For instance, I have the platform resolutions of the Saskatchewan Liberal party adopted at Moose Jaw, June 15-16, 1931. On page 5 I find the following:
Monetary and Banking Reform
The Liberal party, while recognizing that the monetary and banking system is a matter coming wholly within the jurisdiction of the federal parliament, pledges itself:
1.	To encourage and support the establishment of a central bank of rediscount under absolute government control, which central bank should issue all currency.
2.	To advocate the granting to provincial and municipal governments of the right, upon deposit of sound securities, to apply direct to such central bank for currency, the same to be issued to such governments at cost or a minimum rate of interest.
3.	To urge amendment of The Bank Act to provide for the imposition of a penalty on any bank charging more than the legal rate of interest stated in The Bank Act.
4.	To urge that the Canadian dollar be brought to a parity with the British pound sterling.
Of course those were resolutions, but they were circulated among the people of Saskatchewan, who were given the impression
Bank of Canada

that that was the policy of the Liberal party. I have before me another pamphlet which states at the back that the paragraphs therein have been extracted from the official report of the Prime Minister's (Mr. Mackenzie King) speech in the House of Commons on February 27, 1933. Under the heading, "Control of credit," I find the following:
The Liberal party believes that credit is a public matter, not of interest to bankers only, but of direct concern to the average citizen. It stands for the immediate establishment of a properly constituted national central bank, to perform the functions of rediscount, and the control of currency issue, considered in terms of public need. A central bank is necessary to determine the supply of currency in relation to the domestic, social and industrial requirements of the Canadian people; and also to deal with problems of international commerce and exchange.

I have before me another one to which I do not think hon. members opposite will say, "hear, hear." This is headed, "Supplementary platform resolutions of the Saskatchewan Liberal party." They were adopted by the council of the party on January 9-11, 1934. This one states:
Resolved, that this council of the Liberal party of Saskatchewan strongly objects to the capital for the proposed central bank being privately subscribed, and believes that the interests of the people of Canada can best be served by a central bank the capital of which is fully owned and controlled by the government.
I direct the attention of the committee to the words "fully owned." This resolution was circulated throughout the province and the people were given the impression that it constituted the policy and the program of the Liberal party. Not only were these resolutions passed by the rank and file of the Liberal party, but the same idea was encouraged by members of the Liberal party who were acting in a more official capacity. I remember in 1934 when the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. McGeer) came into my riding and told the people that they were going to nationalize the Bank of Canada. Last year the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) came into our fair city, where we were very glad to greet him, and substantiated the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard.

That was true not only outside but inside the house. I am not going to read all the extracts that were cited this afternoon, but one phrase of the hon. member for Waterloo North (Mr. Euler), now Minister of Trade and Commerce, is particularly notable. As reported at page 454 of Hansard of 1935 he made this statement:
We are banding over all our own gold and all the gold of the chartered banks to this privately owned bank and the privilege of issuing currency, though not as much as they should have; moreover they have the control of credit in their hands. I for one do not think that power should remain in the hands of a privately owned bank.
Hon. Charles Stewart, then member for Edmonton West, as reported at page 463 of Hansard of the same year made a similar statement:
We will stand, as the hon. member for North Waterloo has indicated, for public ownership and control of this central bank.
Of course, it may be said that these were expressions of private opinion.. But the fact of the matter is that no attempt was made to tell the public that this was not what the party meant. These expressions were sent through the country broadcast, with the result that, although the Prime Minister may be perfectly correct in his differentiation between terms, there will be a great deal of disappointment in the rank and file of the Liberal party if the resolution as now drawn up is passed as the monetary policy of the government.
With reference to the Prime Minister himself I need hardly waste the time of the house -and I mean that in no derogatory sense- in quoting what most hon. members have already read. In the Vancouver Sun of September 30, 1935, appeared the following:
Mr. Mackenzie King told Vancouver in the Arena, Saturday night, what the Liberal party stands for in this election.
Then there are enumerated ten items. I do not think it is necessary for me to read them;
I will do so if the committee wishes; but number 3 deserves particular notice:
Removal of barriers that prevent credit from serving needs of the people, primarily by nationalizing the central bank.
Number 10 is also very interesting, though, like the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) I may suspect myself to be out of order:
Reduction or abolition of the sales tax on the necessaries of life.

speechtext: I think, however, Mr. Chairman, it is hardly necessary for me to read the quotation. The statement made by the hon. member for Rosthern to-night clarifies the issue considerably. The whole matter boils down to this, then, whether or not all that could be expected from a publicly owned and a publicly controlled bank can be secured through the legislation now being suggested by the Minister of Finance. In other words, if a central bank in which the majority of the shares are held by the government can give the same satisfaction as a publicly owned and publicly controlled central bank, then the people who supported the government on that basis ought to be satisfied. I submit that this will not be the case. The Minister of Finance presented this afternoon an excellent case for a public bank as opposed to a private bank. He pointed out very forcibly that the power of issuing currency and credit was too great to be left in the hands of a few private individuals, or he used words to that effect, and he will correct me if I am not quoting him exactly. Then I maintain that if this power is too great to be left in the hands of a group of private individuals it is also too great to be left in the hands of some individuals appointed by private interests and others appointed by the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS

Well, let us see. I turn to Hansard for 1934, at page 826. The Minister of Finance of that day, Mr. Rhodes, said:
It cannot be too strongly emphasized that the exercise of these functions lies outside the power of any single commercial institution or group of commercial institutions. No purely profit-making institution operating in a competitive system can afford to place social interests before its own in regard to credit policy. This, I think, is obvious. Nor can the management of such a body be expected to regard the maintenance of the monetary standard, for example, as a duty prior to its obligations to the stockholders.
My contention is this: The suggestion of the Minister of Finance is that we should have a board of directors, seven of them private individuals now appointed by the shareholders and fouT with -two votes each to be appointed

by the government, or in other words a voting strength of eight to seven.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

It means that if a time should come when there is a difference between the policy of the government and the policy of those interested in private banks, let us say, a difficult situation may be created. That is quite possible, because I notice in Hansard of February 22, 1934, that Mr. Irvine asked what would happen if there should be a clash between bank policy and government policy. Mr. Rhodes answered:
Unquestionably the authority of the governor and the board of directors of the bank would prevail.
In other words it would seem to me that if enough of the directors appointed by the government could be persuaded to be of the same mind as those appointed by the shareholders there would be a situation in which the policy of the bank would not necessarily be in the interests of the people and the government of the Dominion of Canada. That is quite possible. I notice in the May, 1936, letter of the Royal Bank of Canada, this statement:
Thus, experience gives a measure of proof to the contention which we have repeatedly put forward in these letters, that the violence of the recent depression was due primarily to a deflationary monetary policy and that recovery has been greatly aided by a reversal of that policy.
In the same letter I find this statement:
The real initiative is with the central bank.
In other words with this board of directors lies very largely the welfare of the people of Canada, by reason of the fact that they control the flow of currency and credit which, to use a trite expression, is "the life-blood of the body politic." It seems to me that, if what the Minister of Finance said this afternoon is true-and I believe it is-that those powers are too great to be left in the hands of private individuals privately elected, it is not quite as great a menace, but almost as great, to leave part of that power in the hands of such individuals.

I would suggest that the lamb has been shorn so frequently that it can be picked out quite easily.
I do not wish to prolong the debate, so I simply suggest to the government that across the Dominion of Canada groups within the Liberal party, groups without the Liberal party and people sympathetic to the government are expressing these views. There was a quotation read this morning from the Saskatchewan Liberal. A resolution was read that was passed by a young Liberal club in Saskatoon, all to the same effect. So I ask the government to consider this matter very seriously. To pass the legislation as it is now presented to this house in my opinion will constitute one of the greatest breaches of public faith since confederation. The people of Canada are looking to the government to implement the promises they believe were made, namely to set up a central bank publicly owned and publicly controlled.

subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I was asked by the hon. member sitting directly to my left how a central bank could affect the level of prices, and I told him I would explain later on. As far as may be humanly possible I like to be a man of my word, and I feel called upon to speak again in order to explain that point. In doing so I should like to quote from a very eminent banker, the Right Hon. Reginald McKenna, who has been heard of before in this house. I need not give his record; I will simply quote him:
Nothing in monetary practice is more certain than that contraction in the volume of money or even failure to secure an adequate increase tends both directly and indirectly to put a brake upon business of every kind and to produce the very troubles-unemployment, unremunerative commodity prices, unbalanced budgets and general depression-which have been apparent in almost every country in the world in the past four years. With expanding population and production we need some expansion in the supply of money or it will inevitably follow that consumption will not keep pace with production. There may in any circumstances be temporary maladjustment between production and consumption of individual commodities, but if the supply of money is adequate the price level of all commodities taken together will be kept approximately
stable, and general consumption will be maintained. It follows, then, that the policy of the Bank of England is of the utmost concern to everyone, for no one escapes the effects of general depression and not one of us fails to benefit from sustained prosperity.
That is the way, in the opinion of one of the most eminent bankers in the world, in which the Bank of England operates to raise the level of prices and, as I said a few moments ago, since the Bank of Canada has been set up it has not been operating to raise the level of prices. I think this is sufficiently important to bring to the attention of this house; the Bank of Canada has not been so operating, and it is high time that the government took control of it and made it operate . in that way.
Now I should like to quote the opinion of one of the leading statesmen of the British empire as to one of the causes of the present depression. I wish to read from the considered statement of the Right Hon. Neville Chamberlain to the World Economic Conference which met in London in June, 1933. I read this in order to show that the depression with which we are struggling to-day was deliberately brought about by the financiers of England in order to get back on the gold standard. Probably this quotation is familiar to every member of this house, but I should like to read it again because there may be people who read Hansard to whom it may not be familiar; I think this is something that everyone from one end of Canada to the other should know:
After the termination of the war, we in this country, taking, as it proved, too hopeful a view of world tendencies, set ourselves to restore the pre-war situation. We reestablished budgetary equilibrium and by a long and stern process of deflation we struggled to put sterling back to its pre-war gold parity: at the same time we made every effort to reestablish peaceful relations in Europe and to restore the international gold standard in the countries whose currencies had broken down. In the early part of 1925 Great Britain together with the British empire and certain other countries returned to the gold standard-
I wish hon. members to note that this was apparently decided on without consulting parliament. I mention that because it is time our people realized that these steps in the monetary field sometimes affect them a good deal more than things we spend weeks debating in parliament,

subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
That shows the importance of considering it now. Mr Chamberlain continues:
[DOT]-and although in fact this step entailed further heavy sacrifices for our people in the shape of prolonged unemployment and depression for our industries-
In the face of that strong statement of the Right Hon. Neville Chamberlain that the attempt to deflate, to return to gold, caused further unemployment and further depression to the people of England, can anyone say that this is not important? I ask hon. members to consider what significance that has for us in charting our course for the next four or five years. The question we have to decide is: Are we going to try to do what England did in 1925, try to deflate even more, or are we going to try to introduce an era of easy money and get back to a measure of prosperity?
I wish to read one or two further extracts from this statement to the World Economic Conference which, I think, merit our attention:
The inevitable result of the economic conditions that actually prevailed was to bring about a progressive appreciation of the value of gold, or in other words, a fall in the price of commodities. In certain industrial countries, such as Great Britain and Germany, unemployment became a serious problem.
I ask hon. members who are interested in the primary industries of Western Canada to consider this:
Even more drastic was the effect on countries engaged in primary production, since the fall in price of foodstuffs and raw materials far outstripped the fall in the price of manufactured articles. The situation in the primary producing countries was soon reflected in London as a result of our world-wide trading interests.
The return of England to the gold standard affected the grain farmer in western Canada; it affected the sheep grower in Austrlia, the man raising cattle in western Canada; it affected everyone. They did not know what had happened, but the bankers of England had decided to go back to gold, and every producer of primary products the world over suffered.

There is the statement to the British section of the World Economic Conference. It proceeds later:
It is essential to bring about recovery in the world level of wholesale commodity prices sufficient to yield an economic return to the producers of primary commodities and to restore equilibrium between costs and prices of production generally. It is clear that the present lack of equilibrium between prices and costs can only be remedied either by a further drastic reduction of wages and other costs and by widespread bankruptcies, or by a sufficient recovery in the level of wholesale prices.
That is something for members of parliament to decide: Are they in favour of restoration of the level of prices of say 1928, or are they in favour of further pressing down the primary producers of this country, further bankruptcies, further reductions in wages? It has been suggested to this house already that some wages are too high. Members of parliament have to face that issue. I will not take time to read from the May letter of the Royal Bank of Canada, but in that letter it is stated in so many words that Canada has to face that issue. Is it going in for further deflation or for a period of reflation and easy money and cheap, plentiful credit which will restore industry to the position that it held in 1920-29?
This statement by the British Chancellor continues:
In the opinion of the United Kingdom delefation an attempt to attain equilibrium by urther large reductions of cost would be attended by intolerable suffering, and holds out no hope of success.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
No doubt it would be possible to restore equilibrium between prices and costs by reducing costs if only prices would remain steady. Under present conditions that does not happen but on the contrary an all round reduction in costs produces further deflationary effects on prices, so that costs and prices chase each other downwards without ever getting to equilibrium. Moreover, there is one all-important entity in each country which finds it peculiarly difficult to reduce its own costs-
I direct the attention of the Minister of Finance particularly to this:
-I mean the central government. Every finance minister in the world knows only too well how tremendously resistant public expenditure is to reduction, if only for the reason that so many of its obligations are fixed in terms of money. A policy of reducing costs and prices has the inevitable effect of very greatly reducing the national income with the consequence that in order to balance its accounts the government must take by taxation a larger and larger proportion of the income of the country. Sooner or later, usually sooner, this process is found to be intolerable, and countries bent on securing heavy reductions in costs and prices find that they

Bank of Canada
have merely secured an unbalanced budget for which no practical cure can be found. In the view of the British delegation, therefore, a solution of our present difficulties must be found by means of a recovery in the wholesale price level.
I could go on and quote the opinions of people whose views must carry weight, but I do not intend to take the time to do that. I just wish to indicate that since the Bank of Canada was established we have not followed a policy of easy money; we have followed not a policy of reflation, as they call it in the United States, but rather the opposite.
I wish to give some figures for the consideration of the committee in reference to this. In 1929. in round figures, there was $301.000 000 of legal tender in Canada; in 1936 there was $165,000,000 of legal tender, a reduction of almost fifty per cent. There was also a decrease in bank notes. In 1929. in round figures, there was $142,000,000 worth of bank notes; in 1936, $123,000,000: a reduction of $19 000.000. More important than that, there was a reduction in the amount of credit given to industry, corporations and private individuals with which to carry on business. I am sure hon. members will be amazed, as I was, if they have not looked into this question, to learn that from 1929 to the present time the banks have contracted their loans to corporations and private individuals by the amount of $756,000,000. a contraction of loans to the business world in Canada of 45J per cent from 1929 to 1936. Is it any wonder that we have a depression with such a contraction of the actual money with which people do business? Mr. Jackson Dodds, speaking on November 14. 1935. said:
From a low of $940,000,000 in January, 1926. these current loans steadily rose to $1.588 000 000. in October. 1929. That is an increase of $648,000,000 in forty-five months, or $14.400 000 per month.
The decline from that high point has been much more gradual than the rise, for loans did not recede to $940,000,000 until July of this year. 1935. some sixty-nine months later. Although bank loans are necessarily made for short terms only, it is clear that the banks permitted borrowers to repay these excess loans slowly during a period of five and three-quarter years over 50 per cent longer than their expansion.
What I am trying to indicate is that by virtue of the attempt to bring England back on to gold in 1925. the price level started to topple; as a result banks all over the world began to draw in credit, and as they drew it in, prices toppled still further. It is high time that we took charge of the banking system which under private control has had such disastrous effects upon the whole civilized world, including Canada.
I wish to speak for a moment or so concerning the effect of the curtailment of purchasing power upon prices, and to bear out my observations I shall refer to an extract which contains the figures one would expect, having in mind the contraction in purchasing power. At page 462 of the Labour Gazette of Canada for May, 1936, I find this:
In wholesale prices the index number calculated by the dominion bureau of statistics and based upon prices in 1926 as 190, again showed little change week by week during April as compared with March. This index number was 72-1 for the week ended May 1 as compared with 72-3 the preceding week, and 72-2 for the week ended March 27.
This is the point to which I direct particular attention of hon. members:
On a monthly basis the figures for March, the latest available, are 72-4 as compared with 72-5 for April 1935; 71-3 for April 1934; 63-5 for February 1933, the lowest point in recent years.
It is to be noted that there is a rise from 1933 when the figure stood at 63-5 to 71-3 in April. 1934 and 72-5 in April, 1935, while it stood at 72-4 in March, 1936. In other words, in the last year there has been no gain in the price level. In 1930 it stood at 91-2; it was 98-14 in April of 1922; it was 164-3 in May. 1920. and 64 in April, 1914. These are the figures indicating the price levels as given by the bureau of statistics. When the circulation was increased by the $53,000,000 and the $35.000 000. there was a rise of ten points. During the last year that rise has been absent. On the contrary we have had a slight recession.
should like now to refer to some prices with which some hon. members will be most familiar. Taking the 1926 price of vegetable products as 100 we find that in December, 1932, the figure stood at 50-1; December, 1933, 6J-4; December. 1934, 66-7; December, 1935, 67, or an increase of three-tenths of one point. At that rate we are getting back pretty slowly to the 100 mark. Then, referring to animals and animal products, again taking the 1926 figure as 100. we find the figure for December, 1932, as 57-4; December, 1933, 63-7; December, 1934, 66-2, and December, 1935, 72-9. In the last year it would seem that in connection with animal products there has been a rise of slightly over six points, but we have still eighteen points to go to get back to the level of 1926.
To sum up. I submit that by control of the Bank of Canada, by the use of monetary action and by putting out the requisite amount of money we can affect the level of prices in Canada. The time has long since arrived when the government should take control of the Bank of Canada and without in any way dislocating our economic set-up, by
Bank of Canada

careful monetary action restore the level of wholesale prices in accordance with the recommendations of the Imperial Economic Conference at Ottawa, and the British section of the World Economic Conference at London, and in accordance with the judgments of leading bankers who have made a study of the question.
It is time we broke away from the policy that the only way to create money is to save it. If every hon. member began saving and if we were to cut down consumption to the level adopted by Mr. Ghandi of India, who lives on a little rice and goat's milk and dresses in a loin cloth, our economic set-up would not last very long. It would tumble within six months.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext: We would all be raising goats.

subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
We would not last long in our winter weather, anyway. I submit that our automobile and furniture factories would be closed. All business to the extent it prevails in Canada would be closed up, and yet the basis adopted by the orthodox economist is that we must save and thereby retain the old virtues of thrift and so on. Those old virtues were all right in days when the country was being opened up and when there was a real scarcity of goods, but the situation to-day is different with a plentiful supply of goods. Saving is not as a result so socially beneficial. I submit that we must use the central bank so that the level of prices may be raised, and so that people engaged in industry may have enough money to buy what they have produced.
I have not touched upon another point I suggested earlier in the session. In closing, may I indicate that since coming to this house and further studying monetary questions, with all the intelligence I can bring to bear, I am still of the opinion that in Canada we should support a government bank doing the governmental banking, and that we should set up a branch of the central bank to finance our governments. We should thereupon through it refinance our governmental debt. We could charge interest, if we wished, but such interest would come back to the people in profits of the government bank, thereby cutting down the tremendous burden our people shoulder at this time when they pay interest on their own credit. In this way we would divorce public finance from private finance. Private bankers would continue to do business with business men, but the rate of interest to private business would be cut down, because governments would not be competing

with private business for credit from private banks. I submit that if the private banks can create credit, then our own bank, through a separate department, could create and loan the necessary credit needed to finance our government. In this way we could equate consumption and production and set the wheels of industry turning. As a people we have the greatest chance of any country to produce wealth. We have a people as industrious and skilled as any in the world. We have unparalleled natural resources; we have the factories necessary to produce the wealth, and having those opportunities I submit that it is up to us to use our ability as a people to produce the good things of life and make full use of them by distributing these good things among the people who need them. In other words, to come back to the last word in the Liberal fourteen points, distribution has become more important than production, and it is only just and proper that the Liberal party should bring this measure into parliament. Once we get control of the central bank I hope that it will be only a beginning, and that we shall go forward in the days to come striking off the shackles of economic insecurity from the people of Canada and restoring to them that security and happiness and economic wellbeing to which they as a people are entitled.

This resolution seeks to increase the bank's capital stock, and in such case to purchase the bank's shares in order to ensure a majority holding by the government; also to increase the number of directors and to ensure voting control by the government through its own elected directors. In other words, the resolution seeks to provide the government with the cheap and nasty methods of obtaining control of a successful business which are universally accepted as the peak of ingenious attainment of this object by big business interests. Because big business often uses the public and its employees as suckers is no reason why the government should do the same thing. These are strong words, and I will .admit that I have cast my objection suddenly into the deep end of this matter when I might have approached it with a little more care and gradualness.
